title: Enter a large, existing category instead of inventing a new one
hypothesis: If we pick a large, established category instead of a new one, then early conversion rises because buyers already understand what the product is.
does_not_apply_when: A short trending cash test with no plan to hold inventory for years

signal.check: The team is choosing a category to build a brand in for years, not picking a single trending test item.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source measures a lift

risk.note: A mature category may already have strong incumbents to beat.

prerequisites: A shortlist of candidate categories the brand could enter
steps: List categories that are decades old and bought weekly or monthly.
Drop any category that needs buyers to learn what the product even is.
Check the category has no clearly best loved brand yet.
Pick the category with the clearest gap for a different entry.

test.method: Compare early PDP conversion in the new category against the brand's other launches
test.read_point: after the first 200 sessions on the new PDP

title: Scan the category for a sea of sameness before picking an angle
hypothesis: If we score how identical every competitor in the category looks, then the new product's angle converts better because it stands out where everyone else looks the same.

signal.check: Walking the shelf or the top 20 search results shows near identical packaging, color and claims across incumbents.

risk.note: A sameness read from a small sample can be biased by which stores you look at.

prerequisites: A defined category and country to scan
steps: Walk the physical aisle or the top 20 search results for the category.
Note color, shape, voice and claims used by every incumbent.
Score the category 1 to 5 on how identical it looks.
Log any shopper confusion signal you can observe or hear.

test.method: Track whether the differentiated angle gets asked about or mentioned in reviews after launch

title: Run a brand recall test to find category white space
hypothesis: If we ask target buyers to name their top 3 brands in a category and they cannot, then a new entrant converts better because no incumbent owns the buyer's trust yet.
does_not_apply_when: A category where consumer love is high but the unit economics have not been checked separately

signal.check: 5 to 10 target buyers cannot name 3 brands in the category, or only name the generic product name.

risk.note: Strong consumer love in a white space category does not guarantee the unit economics work.

prerequisites: Access to 5 to 10 people in the target buyer group
steps: Ask 5 to 10 target buyers to name their top 3 brands in the category.
Record how many can name 3, 1, or none.
Treat a low recall rate as an opening, not proof of demand.
Run the unit economics gate before funding the idea on this alone.

test.method: Re-run the same recall question after launch to see if the brand is now named

title: Watch for a shift in how people shop, pay or get delivery
hypothesis: If we build for a shopping, payment or delivery shift that incumbents have not adopted, then new buyers convert more easily because the store already matches what they now expect.

signal.check: A new payment, checkout or delivery expectation is visibly changing PDP or checkout behavior in the category.

risk.note: A shift that looks big in one market may not be visible or wanted in another.

prerequisites: A category and target market already chosen
steps: Write the bridging question: what would a modern version of this category's checkout or delivery look like.
List which incumbents have not adopted that shift yet.
Check whether the brand's platform and payment stack can support it.
Add the shift to the launch plan only if it changes what happens on PDP or checkout.

test.method: A/B the new payment or delivery option on the PDP or checkout
test.read_point: after enough checkout sessions for the brand's own sample size rule

title: Screen every candidate for a felt problem or passionate community
hypothesis: If we require every candidate to solve a daily pain or serve a passionate community, then conversion rises because the offer meets a real, felt need instead of a nice to have.
does_not_apply_when: A candidate with no daily pain and no passionate community behind it, chosen only because the founder likes it

signal.check: A candidate has not yet been scored on whether it solves a daily problem, an occasional problem, or serves a passionate community, or is just a nice to have.

risk.note: Rejecting passion-only products may miss a genuine niche if demand evidence is strong.

prerequisites: A one-line problem statement for the candidate
steps: Write the problem the product solves in one sentence and who feels it.
Rank it: daily pain, occasional pain, passion community, or nice to have.
Drop nice to have candidates unless a passionate community shows strong demand evidence.
Log the rank next to the candidate in the research sheet.

test.method: Compare test CPA and conversion of daily pain candidates against passion only or nice to have candidates over time
test.read_point: after 3 to 5 product tests are logged

title: Pick a broad emotional problem so more products can be tested
hypothesis: If we narrow to a broad emotional problem instead of one narrow symptom, then the number of testable product ideas rises because one problem maps to many possible products.

signal.check: The current product search starts from one narrow product idea instead of a broad felt problem with several possible solutions.

risk.note: A broad problem can produce candidates that do not fit the brand's category.

prerequisites: A market or audience already chosen
steps: Name one broad emotional problem in the market, for example ongoing joint pain.
List every product format that could solve it: supplement, wearable, device, cream.
Score each format on demand and margin before choosing one to pursue.
Keep the other formats logged as future candidates.

test.method: Track how many of the logged formats from one problem reach a validated go decision

title: Pair strong demand with a quality gap in existing reviews
hypothesis: If we target a sub-niche with high sales volume and a low average review rating, then conversion rises because the new product fixes what buyers already complain about.
does_not_apply_when: A dropshipping resale of the same item with no ability to change the product

signal.check: A sub-niche shows strong search or sales volume alongside an average rating of about 3.8 or below on a major marketplace.

risk.note: A low rating can reflect shipping or seller issues, not the product design itself.

prerequisites: Access to a marketplace listing with visible ratings for the sub-niche
steps: Find sub-niches with high volume inside the target category.
Read the average rating for each sub-niche's top listings.
Flag any sub-niche at about 3.8 or below as a quality gap opportunity.
Open the negative reviews and list the specific complaints to fix in the spec.

test.method: Compare the new product's review rating against the sub-niche average after launch

title: Ground every pain point in a specific review, not a category post
hypothesis: If we ground each pain point in a specific product review, return reason or support ticket, then the resulting product spec converts better because it answers a real, named complaint.

signal.check: A pain point list came from an AI summary or a general category discussion, not from a specific review naming the product and a complaint.

risk.note: Cherry picking a few loud reviews can misrepresent the average buyer's real complaint.

prerequisites: A candidate product or category with visible reviews
steps: Pull a batch of PDP reviews, return reasons or support tickets for the product or its closest match.
Confirm each pain point names the product, not just the topic.
Cluster the confirmed pain points by theme and rank by how often they appear.
Open the source of any AI suggested pain point and confirm it is real before using it.

test.method: Track whether the copy or spec built from these pain points reduces return or refund reasons tied to the same complaint

title: Match the product category to the revenue model you want
hypothesis: If we choose a category whose real usage pattern fits the revenue model we want, then repeat rate or order volume moves in that direction because the product's real use matches the business model.

signal.check: The brand wants subscription revenue or high one-off volume but has not checked whether the category's real usage supports that pattern.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one operator's example was 33 percent subscribed on one product

risk.note: This is a preference signal, not a guarantee; one store in the source had 0 subscribers despite the category fit.

prerequisites: A shortlist of categories and the business model preference
steps: State whether the goal is subscription revenue or high volume one-off sales.
Check which categories in the shortlist naturally renew or get bought once.
Prefer consumable or renewable formats for a subscription goal.
Prefer one-off, higher-volume formats where fewer sellers compete for that model.

test.method: Track subscription attach rate or repeat order rate by category after launch

title: Prefer products that are scarce offline and absent from big retail
hypothesis: If we prefer products that are hard to find in local stores or big box retail, then paid acquisition works better because buyers have no free, instant alternative to price check against.

signal.check: The candidate product is easy to find at a local store or a big box retailer in the target country.

risk.note: Neither source gives a fallback plan if the product is easy to find offline but still chosen.

prerequisites: A defined target country
steps: Search local retailers and big box chains in the target country for the exact product.
Score the product high if it is scarce offline, low if it is easy to find.
For an easy to find product, require a stronger owned difference before proceeding.
Log the offline availability score with the candidate.

test.method: Compare ROAS between launched products that were offline scarce and ones that were not
test.read_point: after the first full test window per product

title: Replace founder taste with a demand check before funding a candidate
hypothesis: If we require a demand check before funding any candidate the founder personally likes, then wasted spend on unvalidated products falls because the decision is based on evidence, not preference.
does_not_apply_when: Choosing between 2 or 3 concepts that already passed the demand and economics checks equally

signal.check: A candidate is being funded mainly because the founder personally likes it, with no demand check run yet.

risk.note: Over applying this can strip out founder conviction that later proves useful as a tiebreaker.

prerequisites: A candidate proposed on preference alone
steps: Flag any candidate whose only stated reason is founder preference.
Run the demand check on search volume, trend direction and ad library count before any spend.
Check the store's own conversion and repeat purchase data for adjacent products as a second signal.
Only fund the candidate if it clears the demand check, not on preference alone.

test.method: Compare hit rate of founder preference candidates against demand checked candidates
test.read_point: after 5 or more product tests are logged

title: Score customization as a plus only if fulfillment can handle it
hypothesis: If we only score a customizable product positively when the 3PL or supplier can actually fulfil per order customization, then fulfillment delays and returns fall because customization is not promised without the capacity to deliver it.
does_not_apply_when: The 3PL or supplier cannot handle per order customization

signal.check: A candidate offers personalization such as photo, engraving or custom size, and its fulfillment capacity for that has not been confirmed.

risk.note: Personalized items can still generate more returns and support tickets than standard SKUs even when fulfillment can handle them.

prerequisites: A 3PL or supplier relationship to ask
steps: Ask the 3PL or supplier directly whether they can handle per order customization.
Get a real lead time and error rate estimate for customized orders.
Score customization as a plus in the shortlist only if the answer is yes.
If the answer is no, drop customization as a claimed feature.

test.method: Track fulfillment lead time and return rate on customized SKUs after launch

title: Run every trend tool idea through the same demand and margin checks
hypothesis: If we run every idea sourced from a trend tool through the same demand, competition and margin checks as any other candidate, then fewer unvalidated products reach spend because trend tools only supply names, not proof.

signal.check: An idea from a trend tool such as Exploding Topics is being shortlisted without running it through the standard demand, competition and margin checks.

risk.note: This only adds a check, it does not remove any source of ideas.

prerequisites: A trend tool or list producing candidate names
steps: Treat every trend tool hit as a name only, not a validated idea.
Run the same platform demand check, ad library count and landed cost margin check used on any other candidate.
Only add it to the shortlist after it clears those checks.

test.method: Track what share of trend tool candidates pass the full check versus other sources

title: Screen a marketplace listing against that marketplace's own density and fees
hypothesis: If we screen a marketplace-heavy candidate against that marketplace's own listing density, search ranking and take rate, then margin holds because the fee and competition structure there differs from Meta or TikTok Shop.

signal.check: The brand sells or plans to sell a candidate on a marketplace such as Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho, Myntra or Etsy, but has only checked demand on Meta or TikTok Shop.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: Marketplace fee structures and search ranking rules change without notice.

prerequisites: Access to the target marketplace's listing search and fee schedule
steps: Search the marketplace's own listing pages for the exact product and count active competitors.
Look up the marketplace's current take rate and any category specific fees.
Check how search ranking works on that marketplace, not on Meta or TikTok Shop.
Re-run the margin gate using the marketplace's fees instead of a paid social assumption.

test.method: Track actual take home margin per order on the marketplace listing against the assumed margin

title: Filter a video commerce sales tool to a mid-size revenue band
hypothesis: If we filter a video commerce sales tool to a mid-size 30-day revenue band instead of the biggest sellers, then the shortlist avoids the most contested products and ad costs stay lower.
does_not_apply_when: A branded brand that will not source the exact listed product, only read the category for trend and format

signal.check: A video commerce sales tool such as Kalodata is being screened without a defined revenue band, or is including products above about 300000 dollars a month.

expected_effect.size: about 33000 to 97000 dollars a month starting band, self adjust to about 40000 after a failed low band test

risk.note: The band is one operator's live adjusted heuristic, not a measured result.

prerequisites: Access to a video commerce sales data tool
steps: Open the tool's product list for the last 30 days, one category at a time.
Set the revenue range to about 33000 to 97000 dollars, video revenue only.
Avoid products earning 300000 dollars or more a month.
If a product near the floor later fails a live test, raise the floor to about 40000 for the next search.

test.method: Track CPA on products sourced from inside versus outside this revenue band
test.read_point: after each product's short paid test

title: Count video revenue only and reject high live-stream revenue
hypothesis: If we count only video revenue and reject candidates with high live-stream revenue, then a static or short video ad test performs better because live-stream sales do not transfer to a replicable video ad.

signal.check: A video commerce candidate's revenue figure has not been split between video and live-stream sources.

expected_effect.size: reject live revenue at about 25000 dollars or more

risk.note: One operator's threshold, not independently confirmed.

prerequisites: A video commerce tool that splits revenue by source
steps: Switch the tool's revenue source filter to video only.
Check the live-stream revenue figure separately.
Reject the candidate if live revenue is about 25000 dollars or more a month.

test.method: Track video ad ROAS on products that passed this filter versus ones that did not
test.read_point: after each product's short paid test

title: Screen video commerce candidates by graph shape before the product image
hypothesis: If we screen candidates by their revenue graph shape before looking at the product image, then more genuinely undiscovered products get considered because image recognition bias is removed from the first pass.

signal.check: Candidates are being screened by browsing product images first, before checking whether the revenue graph is flat, rising or falling.

risk.note: This only changes the order of an existing screen.

prerequisites: A video commerce tool with a sortable product list
steps: Sort the product list lowest to highest revenue inside the chosen band.
Look only at each row's small revenue graph on the first pass.
Keep graphs that are flat or tilting up at the end and drop straight downtrends.
Only after this pass, look at the product image, and only as a familiarity check.

test.method: Track how many of the shortlisted products were previously unrecognized by the researcher

title: Always check the 180-day graph before deciding on a video commerce candidate
hypothesis: If we always check the 180-day sales graph before deciding on a candidate, then fewer products that already peaked or have no history get funded because the 30-day view alone hides both cases.

signal.check: A candidate is being decided on the 30-day graph alone, without opening the 180-day view.

expected_effect.size: unknown, flagged as the single most common mistake in the source

risk.note: A steep new curve with no history is a gamble either way; this check reduces but does not remove that risk.

prerequisites: A video commerce tool with a 180-day product detail view
steps: Open the 180-day graph for every candidate that passes the 30-day screen.
Reject a product that peaked months ago and now flatlines or declines.
Reject a flat line with no movement.
Keep an up-down-up pattern with an overall rise as the healthiest signal.
Mark a steep, uninterrupted new curve with no prior history as a gamble, not a validated winner.

test.method: Compare test outcomes for products with established up and down history versus brand new steep spikes

title: Check that revenue spreads across several recent videos, not one old one
hypothesis: If we require revenue to spread across 3 to 5 recent videos instead of one old video, then the candidate is more likely to be a repeatable video ad win, not a one-off fluke.

signal.check: A candidate's revenue has not been checked against the last 7 days video list, only lifetime totals.

expected_effect.size: reject when 90 to 95 percent of revenue comes from one video over 7 to 14 days old

risk.note: A single very recent high revenue video can still be worth testing outside this rule, per the source's own stated exception.

prerequisites: A video commerce tool with a last 7 days video breakdown
steps: Open the last 7 days video list for the candidate, not just the lifetime top video.
Confirm the top video by revenue is 7 to 14 days old.
Confirm revenue spreads across 3 to 5 videos, not 90 to 95 percent on one.
If the exception applies, a very large 7-day figure on one video, log the exception and the number before proceeding.

test.method: Track hit rate of products with spread video revenue versus concentrated revenue

title: Require winning creative to be in the target market's language
hypothesis: If we require a candidate's top performing video to be in the target market's own language, then the demand signal is real for that market because a foreign language top ad usually means the product sells elsewhere, not here.

signal.check: A candidate's top video is in a different language than the target market being tested.

risk.note: This only screens out a false signal for one market; it says nothing about the product's demand in the video's actual market.

prerequisites: Ability to watch the candidate's top video
steps: Watch the top performing video for the candidate.
Check whether the language matches the target market's primary language.
If it does not match, skip the product for this market only.
Note the actual market it may fit instead, for a future test.

test.method: Track ad performance for products screened this way against ones that were not
test.read_point: after each product's short paid test

title: Widen category filters before abandoning a niche in a sales data tool
hypothesis: If we widen or switch category filters before leaving a niche empty-handed, then more real candidates surface because a tool's own category bucket is not the same as the product's true niche.

signal.check: A category filter in a sales or ad data tool returns few or no results for a niche known to have real products in it.

risk.note: None; this only broadens a search that already returned nothing.

prerequisites: A sales or ad data tool with adjustable category filters
steps: If a category returns nothing after several pages, try an adjacent category bucket for the same product type.
Fall back to manual keyword or symptom search before concluding the niche is empty.
Only switch niche entirely if the widened search still returns nothing.

test.method: Track how many extra candidates a widened search produces versus the original category filter
test.read_point: at the end of each research session

title: Treat one platform's demand data as a lead, not proof, for a different platform
hypothesis: If we treat demand data from a platform the brand does not advertise on as a lead rather than proof, then fewer products fail their first paid test because platform-specific demand does not always transfer.
does_not_apply_when: The brand advertises directly on the same platform the demand data came from

signal.check: A candidate is validated mainly on demand data from a platform the brand does not run ads on.

risk.note: Weighting demand data from the brand's own platform directly still needs its own margin and competition checks.

prerequisites: The brand's primary ad platform is known
steps: Confirm which platform the brand actually runs paid ads on.
If the demand data came from a different platform, log the product as a candidate only, not a validated pick.
Note in the log when a product is strong on one platform and thin on the brand's own, as an untapped signal.
Run a short test with the brand's own ad, offer and platform before drawing conclusions.

test.method: Compare hit rate of cross-platform leads against same-platform validated candidates

title: Use ad run length as a screen for a live, funded test, not proof of profit
hypothesis: If we require a minimum ad run length before treating a competitor's product as validated, then fewer untested candidates get funded because a long-running ad shows real spend behind it.

signal.check: A candidate's competitor ads have not been checked for how long they have been actively running.

expected_effect.size: strict bar of about 14 days currently running, more than about 1 week for an ad library match

risk.note: Run length is not proof of ROAS; no source shows that link directly.

prerequisites: Access to the ad library or a spy tool that shows run length
steps: Open the advertiser's page transparency or the spy tool's run length column.
Require at least 14 days currently running in a paid spy tool, or more than about a week in the free ad library.
Mark an ad running only hours as no signal yet, bookmark it and watch, do not treat it as proof or a non-threat.
Log the run length with the candidate.

test.method: Compare test outcomes for products backed by 14-day-plus ads against shorter-run ads

title: Read a high concurrent ad count as budget and confidence, then check revenue
hypothesis: If we treat a high active ad count as budget and confidence rather than proof of profit, then fewer candidates are wrongly validated because active ad count alone does not confirm the seller is profitable.

signal.check: A candidate is being validated mainly because a competitor is running many active ads at once.

risk.note: None; this only adds a required second check.

prerequisites: Access to a tool that reports active ads per advertiser page
steps: Note the active ad count per advertiser as a confidence signal only.
Always follow with a revenue estimate before treating the advertiser as proof.
Do not shortlist a candidate on ad count alone.

test.method: Track how many high-ad-count candidates also clear the revenue floor
test.read_point: at the end of each research session

title: Search the ad library with generic offer and problem phrases
hypothesis: If we search the ad library with generic offer phrases and problem terms instead of exact product names, then more direct-response competitors and candidate products surface for free.

signal.check: Ad library scouting has only used exact product names, not generic offer or symptom phrases.

risk.note: Category filters under-include; a manual keyword fallback may still be needed.

prerequisites: Access to the Meta ad library for the target country
steps: Set the ad library to the target country and active ads only.
Search generic offer phrases such as free shipping, 50 percent off, shop now.
Search problem phrases such as a symptom or pain point term.
Optionally limit to the last 1 to 2 weeks to bias toward new tests, and also search the category term itself for branded competitors.

test.method: Track how many usable candidates come from keyword search versus exact product name search
test.read_point: at the end of each research session

title: Fall back to manual keyword search when a category filter returns nothing
hypothesis: If we search manual symptom or problem keywords when a category filter returns junk, then real competitors surface because tool categories under-include obvious matches.

signal.check: A spy tool or ad library category filter returns mostly irrelevant results for a known real niche.

risk.note: Manual keyword search is slower than a category filter.

prerequisites: A list of symptom or problem keywords for the niche
steps: If category filters return junk, switch to manual keyword search using symptom or problem terms.
Search the exact category term as well as related symptom terms.
Log which search terms actually produced usable candidates for next time.

test.method: Compare candidate yield from category filters versus manual keyword search on the same niche
test.read_point: at the end of each research session

title: Study established brand advertisers for the gap they leave, not to copy them
hypothesis: If a branded brand studies established mega-brand advertisers for what avatar or angle they do not serve instead of skipping them, then a genuine positioning gap is more likely to be found because incumbents define what is already served.
does_not_apply_when: A dropshipping-style resale model with no owned brand to differentiate

signal.check: Spy tool or ad library scans are skipping heavily branded, established advertisers instead of reading them for unserved angles.

risk.note: Mega brand ads can be harder to interpret since they may not run pure direct-response creative.

prerequisites: A list of established brand advertisers in the category
steps: List the mega brands already advertising heavily in the category.
Catalogue the avatars, outcomes and offers their ads already serve.
Write what type of customer or occasion none of them address.
Use this gap as an input to the angle audit, not as a product to copy.

test.method: Track whether angles sourced from incumbent-gap analysis convert better than copied angles
test.read_point: after the first test of the new angle

title: Cap results per advertiser and widen the results page in a spy tool
hypothesis: If we cap ads per advertiser and set a large results page size in a spy tool, then the scan surfaces more distinct competitors because one heavy advertiser cannot flood the list.

signal.check: A spy tool scan is not capping ads per advertiser or is using a small results page size.

expected_effect.size: cap of about 4 ads per brand, 500 results per page

risk.note: Filter names and limits in these tools change without notice.

prerequisites: Access to a paid ad spy tool
steps: Set the ads-per-brand cap to about 4 to prevent one advertiser flooding the list.
Set the results per page to about 500 to speed the scan.
Re-check these settings periodically since spy tool UIs change.

test.method: Track number of distinct advertisers surfaced per scan before and after applying these settings
test.read_point: at the end of each research session

title: Rate each competitor's store and offer, not just their ad
hypothesis: If we rate each competitor's actual store and offer instead of only their ad, then the competition count is more accurate because a generic weak store counts as a beatable competitor, not a serious one.

signal.check: Competitors are being counted from ads alone without opening their stores to check offer and build quality.

risk.note: A store that has stopped running the product should not count toward saturation.

prerequisites: A list of competitor stores from the ad scan
steps: Open each competitor's store from their ad.
Rate the store beatable or serious based on template quality, subscription offer and bundle strength.
Note the offer structure used, such as BOGO or a named bundle.
Exclude stores that have stopped running the product from the saturation count.

test.method: Track whether competitor counts that include store quality predict test outcomes better than ad counts alone

title: Mine a validated competitor's top ad for avatar and angle, never the asset
hypothesis: If we mine a competitor's longest-running ad for the avatar and message frame in words only, then a new angle can be built without legal or brand risk because no asset, text, logo or face is ever reused.

signal.check: A competitor's ad is being screenshotted, downloaded or closely mimicked instead of studied for avatar and angle in words.

risk.note: Describing an angle in words still requires the creative team to execute it well to actually convert.

prerequisites: A validated competitor ad identified by run length and revenue
steps: Find the competitor's longest-running or highest-impression ad.
Write down the avatar, situation and message frame in plain words.
Never download, remix or repost the actual ad asset, text, logo or face.
Hand the written angle brief to the creative team to build fresh, original assets.

test.method: Track whether angle briefs built this way produce usable creative without any IP flags

title: Scout native ad widgets for older-buyer problem categories
hypothesis: If we scan native paid-content widgets on general-interest sites for recurring older-buyer problem categories, then new candidate products surface for a 60-plus, Facebook-led audience that other scouting methods miss.
does_not_apply_when: The brand does not serve or want to serve buyers aged 60 or older

signal.check: The brand serves or wants to serve buyers aged 60 or older on Facebook, and native widget scouting has not been tried.

risk.note: Whether these placements still exist and still skew older is unverified and should be checked live.

prerequisites: Confirmation that the brand's audience skews 60 or older
steps: Open a general-interest news or weather site known to carry paid content blocks.
Refresh the block repeatedly and log every product and problem that recurs.
Rate each problem on severity and privacy sensitivity separately from how good the product looks.
Validate any promising find in the ad library with an image filter and a run length check.

test.method: Track candidate yield and later hit rate from native widget scouting versus other scouting methods

title: Never scrape an aggregator feed or copy a competitor's store outright
hypothesis: If we refuse to scrape saturated aggregator feeds or copy a competitor's store directly, then ad costs stay lower and the brand avoids a race to the bottom because thousands of sellers already work the same feed.

signal.check: A candidate or store design was pulled directly from a saturated aggregator feed or a close copy of one competitor's store.

risk.note: Both cited sources still start research from a competitor's product; the requirement is that something in avatar, geography, offer or research depth must differ.

prerequisites: A candidate sourced from a competitor or an aggregator feed
steps: Check whether the candidate or store concept came from a widely-scraped aggregator feed.
If so, require a real point of difference: a new avatar, geography, offer or deeper research than the field.
Never copy a competitor's store layout, copy or images directly.

test.method: Track CPM trend on products sourced from crowded aggregator feeds versus differentiated entries
test.read_point: after each product's short paid test

title: Train a fresh social account to surface product ads, time-boxed
hypothesis: If we train a fresh TikTok or Instagram account to surface product-pitch content for a time-boxed period, then free candidate discovery happens without paying for a spy tool.
does_not_apply_when: The brand's primary platform is not TikTok or Instagram

signal.check: No free organic scouting method is running, and the team has time for short, frequent sessions on a fresh account.

risk.note: The feed can drift off-topic or return mostly reposts; time-box the effort and switch method if it stops working.

prerequisites: A fresh social account used only for research
steps: On TikTok, watch fully and like every product-pitch video, keep scrolling until the feed is mostly pitches.
On Instagram, search a winning-product hashtag, like 5 to 10 physical-product videos, then switch to Reels and keep liking.
Run short, frequent sessions rather than one long session, and prefer mobile.
Time-box the method to about 2 weeks; if it only returns reposts, switch to ad library or spy tool scouting.

test.method: Track candidate yield per session and how many became validated picks

title: Require 3 or more million-view videos before trusting one viral post
hypothesis: If we require at least 3 videos over 1 million views on a creator's profile before treating one viral post as a candidate, then fewer false positives get logged because high views can reflect the creator's personality, not the product.

signal.check: A single viral video is being logged as a candidate without checking the creator's other video view counts.

expected_effect.size: require 3 or more videos over 1000000 views

risk.note: This is one operator's personal heuristic, not a measured cutoff.

prerequisites: A viral video candidate found through organic scouting
steps: Open the creator's profile after spotting a viral product video.
Count how many of their videos exceed 1 million views.
Log the candidate only if 3 or more videos clear that bar.
Otherwise, keep scrolling and treat the one video as a fluke.

test.method: Track how many logged candidates that passed this filter later validated versus ones that did not use the filter

title: Stop scrolling and log a candidate the moment it passes the basic screen
hypothesis: If researchers log a candidate the moment it shows a sellable product with a visible price and offer, then research time is used more efficiently because more scrolling only delays validation, it does not improve the shortlist.

signal.check: A researcher keeps scrolling past qualifying candidates looking for a better one instead of logging and moving to validation.

risk.note: None; this only changes when a candidate is logged, not the screening bar itself.

prerequisites: A research log to record candidates in
steps: The moment a scouted post shows a sellable product with a visible price and offer that meets the basic screen, stop scrolling.
Log it immediately with source, price and a link or screenshot reference.
Move to the next candidate or to validation rather than continuing to scroll for something better.

test.method: Track time from first sighting to logged candidate before and after this rule
test.read_point: over one week of active hunting

title: Require existing content or an easy on-camera demo before betting on a product
hypothesis: If we require either existing footage or an easy 15-second on-camera demo before committing to a product, then creative production is not blocked because the product cannot be shown clearly on video.
does_not_apply_when: The product is a service, digital good or has no visual demonstration at all

signal.check: A candidate has no existing TikTok or social footage and it is unclear whether it can be demoed on camera quickly.

risk.note: A branded brand can plan a shoot rather than dropping the product outright, unlike a pure dropshipping model.

prerequisites: A candidate that has cleared the basic problem or passion screen
steps: Search TikTok and social platforms for existing footage of the product or a close match.
If none exists, ask whether the product can be clearly demoed on camera in under 15 seconds.
For a branded brand, plan a content shoot rather than dropping the candidate outright.
Log the content plan or existing footage links with the candidate.

test.method: Track creative production time and cost for products that passed this gate versus ones that did not

title: Track whether a seeded creator's post actually drives sales before calling it validated
hypothesis: If we track sales tied to a seeded creator's post instead of assuming it validates the product, then fewer products are wrongly greenlit because seeding is a demand and content method distinct from organic scouting, not proof on its own.

signal.check: A product was seeded to a creator and the resulting post's engagement is being treated as validated demand without a sales link.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: Engagement on a seeded post can be inflated by the creator's own following, not real buyer intent.

prerequisites: A creator seeding program or a plan to start one
steps: Give each seeded post a trackable link or discount code.
Record views, engagement and actual sales tied to the post separately.
Treat the product as validated only if sales followed, not just engagement.
Log the seeded creator result alongside other demand evidence for the candidate.

test.method: Compare conversion rate of seeded-post traffic against the store's average traffic
test.read_point: 2 weeks after the seeded post goes live

title: Delegate research-heavy steps to an AI agent, keep go or no-go decisions human
hypothesis: If we delegate trend scanning, review mining and first-pass concepts to an AI agent while keeping build, supplier and order-size decisions human, then research throughput rises because the founder's time is spent only on decisions that need judgment.

signal.check: A founder or researcher is spending hours on trend scanning, review mining or sub-niche listing that an AI agent could do faster.

risk.note: AI sourcing ends at a validated, margin-checked product; it should not write ads, manage bids or fix checkout.

prerequisites: Access to an AI research assistant
steps: List which research steps are mechanical: trend scanning, review mining, pain-point clustering, sub-niche lists, first-pass concepts.
Hand those steps to the AI agent with clear prompts and expected outputs.
Keep the decision to build, the supplier calls and the order size as human decisions.
Review the AI's output for accuracy before acting on it.

test.method: Track hours spent per validated candidate before and after delegating research steps

title: Generate a long list of emotional sub-niches, then narrow to a working few
hypothesis: If we ask an AI assistant to generate about 30 emotional sub-niches inside a market and then pick 5, then the research scope is both broad and workable because the list surfaces angles a person would not brainstorm alone.

signal.check: Sub-niche selection for a market is starting from only 1 or 2 ideas instead of a generated long list.

expected_effect.size: about 30 generated, 5 chosen, from one operator

risk.note: The exact prompt used in the source is not available; build one from the inputs and outputs needed.

prerequisites: A chosen market to search sub-niches within
steps: Ask the AI assistant for about 30 emotional sub-niches inside the chosen market, each stated as a felt problem with who feels it and when.
Review the list for sub-niches that fit the brand's category and audience.
Pick 5 sub-niches to use as the research scope for the next step.
Log the full list for future research cycles.

test.method: Track how many of the 5 chosen sub-niches produce a validated candidate

title: Treat AI-generated concepts and mockups as stimulus, not a sourcing spec
hypothesis: If we combine an AI-generated concept with ranked, cited pain points before writing the real spec, then supplier quotes come back accurate because the factory never works from an unverified mockup alone.

signal.check: An AI-generated mockup or concept is being sent to a supplier or factory without being combined with cited, ranked pain points.

risk.note: Sending an unverified AI mockup straight to a factory risks a wasted sample run.

prerequisites: An AI-generated concept or mockup for the candidate
steps: Treat the AI concept or mockup as a starting stimulus only.
Combine it with the ranked, cited pain points from review or forum mining.
Write the real product specification from the combined input.
Never send the raw mockup to a factory as the spec.

test.method: Track supplier quote accuracy and revision count for specs built this way versus mockup-only specs

title: Mine reviews for a price buyers say they would actually pay
hypothesis: If we search reviews for a buyer naming a price they would pay or a competitor price they found too high, then the price band is set more accurately because it is the closest proxy to real willingness to pay before a live listing exists.

signal.check: A price band is being set from a source's example numbers instead of buyer statements found in reviews or forums.

risk.note: Review-mentioned prices are self-selected and can skew toward complaints, not typical buyers.

prerequisites: A set of reviews, forum posts or Q&A for the product or its closest match
steps: Search reviews and forum posts for a buyer naming a price they would pay.
Search for mentions of a competitor price found too high.
Search for any pre-order or waitlist pledge amount.
Use these mentions as one input to the price band, alongside the comparable-products check.

test.method: Compare the review-derived price expectation against actual conversion at the chosen launch price

title: Re-check an AI-sourced brand's revenue before treating ad volume as proof
hypothesis: If we run a revenue estimate on every AI-sourced brand before treating its active ad volume as validation, then fewer weak candidates are shortlisted because ad volume can reflect budget or testing, not profit.

signal.check: An AI research agent has flagged a brand as qualified based on active ad volume, without a revenue estimate run yet.

risk.note: None; this only adds a required second check after an AI-generated shortlist.

prerequisites: An AI-generated shortlist of brands with active ad counts
steps: Treat any AI-flagged brand as a candidate, not proof.
Run the standard competitor revenue estimate on each flagged brand.
Only keep brands that clear the revenue floor or have a second independent seller.

test.method: Track what share of AI-flagged candidates pass the revenue check

title: Cross-check keyword volume and mentions against the ad library before shortlisting
hypothesis: If we cross-check keyword volume and social mentions against ad library activity before shortlisting, then fewer candidates with high interest but no buying intent get funded because search and mention counts alone do not confirm anyone will check out.

signal.check: A candidate's demand case rests only on keyword volume or social mention counts, with no ad library cross-check.

risk.note: None; this only adds a required cross-check.

prerequisites: Access to a keyword volume tool and the ad library
steps: Pull keyword search volume for the core terms from a keyword planner.
Pull daily social mention counts from a mention-tracking tool if available.
Cross-check against the ad library for active advertisers on the same term.
Only proceed to a full demand check if both sides show real activity.

test.method: Track how often keyword-only candidates fail the full demand check versus cross-checked ones

title: Run a 12-month trend check on the exact sub-niche term
hypothesis: If we run a 12-month trend check on the exact sub-niche term instead of the parent category term, then a rising format is not missed because a parent term at an all-time high can hide a sub-format still on a fresh rise.

signal.check: A trend check has been run on the broad category term instead of the exact sub-niche or product format term.

risk.note: A 12-month window alone can miss a fad that has not yet peaked; pair with the multi-year check.

prerequisites: The exact sub-niche or product format term identified
steps: Search the exact sub-niche term, not the parent category, in a trend tool.
Set the window to 12 months.
Require an active current uptrend before proceeding.
If conviction is already very high from other evidence, this check can be skipped, but log that decision.

test.method: Track hit rate of candidates with a confirmed 12-month uptrend versus those without

title: Run a multi-year trend check to separate a fad from real growth
hypothesis: If we plot several years of trend data on the exact sub-niche term, then we avoid committing inventory to a fad because a multi-year view separates a growing category from a spike that always reverses.

signal.check: Only a 12-month trend window has been checked, with no multi-year view to classify growing, flat, fad or declining.

expected_effect.size: classify growing, flat, fad or declining over several years

risk.note: This check is required in the source, not optional like the 12-month view.

prerequisites: A trend tool with multi-year history for the term
steps: Search the same exact sub-niche term over 5 years or the tool's maximum history.
Classify the shape as growing, flat, fad or declining.
Mark any recurring monthly spikes as seasonality, not fad.
Drop a fad-shaped candidate unless it is explicitly run as a short trending cash test.

test.method: Track inventory write-off rate on products with confirmed multi-year growth versus fad-shaped ones

title: Read trend direction and competitor count together, not separately
hypothesis: If we read trend direction and ad library competitor count as one combined signal instead of separately, then entry timing improves because a crowded and fading market is a late entry while an empty and rising one may be early or unproven.

signal.check: Trend direction and competitor count are being scored separately with no combined read to decide entry timing.

risk.note: An empty library with a rising trend is ambiguous; use the positioning gap check to resolve it.

prerequisites: Both a trend read and a competitor count for the candidate
steps: Plot the trend direction: rising, flat or fading.
Plot the competitor count: crowded or open.
Combine them: crowded plus rising is the best combination, crowded plus fading is a late entry, empty plus rising is early or unproven.
For empty plus rising, run the positioning gap check before deciding.

test.method: Track hit rate by combined trend and competition quadrant across tested products

title: Plan a secondary evergreen product before betting inventory on a trend
hypothesis: If we plan a secondary evergreen SKU before committing MOQ inventory to a trend-led pick, then cash risk falls because a rising trend can reverse before the first inventory order sells through.
does_not_apply_when: A trending pick run as a fixed-budget cash test with no inventory purchase

signal.check: An MOQ order is planned for a trend-led hero SKU with no secondary evergreen product named yet.

risk.note: An MOQ order already placed against a trend cannot be undone if the trend reverses.

prerequisites: A trend-led hero SKU candidate approaching an MOQ order
steps: Before placing the MOQ order, name at least one evergreen secondary product in the same category.
Sketch the trigger for launching the secondary product, such as the hero's first reorder or a set revenue milestone.
Only place the MOQ order once the secondary plan exists on paper.

test.method: Track inventory sell-through rate on hero SKUs launched with a secondary plan versus without

title: Require search volume and unit sales to move together before treating a spike as a permanent SKU
hypothesis: If we require search volume and unit sales to move together and hold before treating a candidate as a permanent catalog SKU, then fewer over-ordered SKUs sit as dead stock because a spike with no matching sales is a one-batch signal, not a stable demand signal.

signal.check: A candidate's search volume is rising but unit sales data has not been checked to see if it moves the same way.

risk.note: Sales data may not be available before a live listing exists, forcing a judgment call.

prerequisites: Access to a tool that shows both search volume and sales count over time
steps: Chart search volume and unit sales for the sub-niche over the same period.
Check whether they move together and hold, or whether volume spikes with no matching sales.
If they move together, treat it as fit for a permanent catalog SKU.
If volume spikes without sales, plan one limited batch, not an MOQ order or full PDP build.

test.method: Track sell-through rate on SKUs launched after this check versus without it

title: Estimate competitor revenue and apply a floor before treating them as proof
hypothesis: If we estimate a competitor's monthly revenue and apply a floor before treating them as proof of a viable product, then fewer products are validated on ad volume alone because active ads can be budget or testing, not profit.

signal.check: A single competitor is being treated as proof of demand with no revenue estimate run and no second independent seller found.

expected_effect.size: floor of roughly 200000 to 300000 dollars a month for a single competitor to count as proof

risk.note: The floor is stated 2 different ways by the same source and is one operator's number, not a measured result.

prerequisites: A traffic estimation tool such as a browser extension
steps: Install a traffic estimation tool and read the competitor's estimated monthly visits, taking the conservative figure.
Choose a conversion rate of about 2 percent baseline, lower for higher ticket items.
Estimate AOV conservatively from the visible offer stack.
Multiply visits by rate by AOV, and apply the roughly 200000 to 300000 dollar floor, or require a second independent seller below it.

test.method: Track hit rate of products validated above the revenue floor versus below it with only 1 seller

title: Treat no traffic data as ambiguous, not proof a store is dead
hypothesis: If we treat a traffic tool showing no data for a competitor store as ambiguous rather than a dead store, then fewer real, small or new competitors get wrongly dismissed because the tool usually just means low visit volume.

signal.check: A candidate or competitor is being dropped because a traffic estimation tool shows no data for their store.

expected_effect.size: unknown, usually means a new or under 5000 visit store

risk.note: None; this only prevents a wrong drop decision.

prerequisites: A traffic estimation tool showing no data for a store
steps: When a traffic tool shows no data, do not drop the candidate on that alone.
Check the ad library for the same store to confirm whether ads are actively running.
Look for other signals such as recent reviews or social activity before deciding.

test.method: Track how many no-data competitors were later confirmed active through other signals
test.read_point: at the end of each research session

title: Confirm the target buyer is reachable, online and shippable before sourcing
hypothesis: If we confirm the target buyer's country, online buying habit and shipping feasibility before sourcing, then fewer products are sourced for a buyer the store cannot actually reach or ship to.

signal.check: A candidate's target buyer country, online-buying behavior and shipping feasibility have not been explicitly checked.

risk.note: Audience tools once used for this, such as Alexa, are discontinued; a current replacement must be chosen and recorded.

prerequisites: A defined target country and buyer profile
steps: Check trend tool region data to confirm where interest is coming from.
Sample social profiles engaging with the category to confirm the buyer profile.
Confirm the buyer typically buys online in that country.
Confirm the store can ship to that country at an acceptable cost and time.

test.method: Track order fulfillment success rate by target country against the reachability check result
test.read_point: first 90 days after launch in that country

title: Grade competitor count in the free ad library with a green amber red ladder
hypothesis: If we grade the exact-product competitor count in the free ad library with a green, amber, red ladder, then entry decisions are more consistent because a second or third identical bidder measurably raises CPMs.

signal.check: A candidate's exact-product competitor count in the target country has not been counted and graded against a fixed ladder.

expected_effect.size: 0 to 1 advertiser is green, 2 to 4 is amber, 5 or more with no angle is red

risk.note: Stores that stopped running the product should not count toward the ladder.

prerequisites: Access to the Meta ad library for the target country
steps: Search the exact product name in the ad library, filtered to the target country and active ads.
Count distinct stores active in the last 7 days.
Grade green for 0 to 1, amber for 2 to 4, red for 5 or more with no differentiation angle.
Route amber or red candidates to the positioning gap audit before proceeding.

test.method: Track average CPM achieved on green, amber and red graded launches
test.read_point: after each product's short paid test

title: Grade competitor count in a paid spy tool with its own total and serious bar
hypothesis: If we grade a candidate's total and serious competitor count inside a paid spy tool separately from the free ad library ladder, then the read is more accurate because the paid tool surfaces a different, usually larger, set of sellers.

signal.check: A candidate has been graded in the free ad library but not checked against a paid spy tool's own store count.

expected_effect.size: pass bar of under about 10 total stores selling it and no more than 3 serious ones

risk.note: One operator's threshold from one paid tool; filter names and counts drift as the tool updates.

prerequisites: Access to a paid ad spy tool with a store-count feature
steps: Search the exact product name in the paid spy tool.
Count total stores selling it and how many look serious, well-built and branded.
Pass if under about 10 total and at most 3 serious.
Route candidates that fail this bar to the positioning gap audit.

test.method: Track hit rate of candidates passing the spy tool bar versus failing it

title: Count niche-level competitors and substitutes, not just the exact product
hypothesis: If we count competitors at the niche level and include substitutes, then the true competition picture is more accurate because buyers compare across formats, not only against the exact product.

signal.check: Only the exact product's competitor count has been checked, with no search for substitutes or adjacent formats solving the same problem.

risk.note: None; this only adds a broader competitor search.

prerequisites: The exact-product competitor count already done
steps: Search the niche term, not just the exact product name.
List substitute formats solving the same problem, such as pills, gummies or powders of the same ingredient.
Include DIY, homemade and generic-commodity alternatives, searched per target country.
Fold the substitute count into the overall competition read.

test.method: Track whether niche-inclusive competition counts predict CPM better than exact-product counts alone

title: Treat saturation as demand proof only with a concrete unserved angle
hypothesis: If we only treat a saturated market as an opportunity when a concrete unserved avatar, geography or offer can be named, then more saturated-market entries succeed because saturation alone proves demand, not a way to win.
does_not_apply_when: No unserved avatar, geography or offer can be named for the candidate

signal.check: A market is being entered because many sellers already prove demand, without a named unserved avatar, geography or offer.

risk.note: A CPM assumption 25 percent above the brand's history is a placeholder until real brand data replaces it.

prerequisites: A red or amber graded competition read for the candidate
steps: Confirm the market is saturated per the competitor ladder.
Run the positioning gap audit to name an unserved avatar, geography or offer.
If an angle exists and the margin gate still passes at a higher assumed CPM, proceed as a differentiated entry.
If no angle can be named, drop the candidate for this brand.

test.method: Track CPM and hit rate on saturated-market entries with a named angle versus without one
test.read_point: after each product's short paid test

title: Treat a product with 10 or more identical sellers as a cash test, not a brand
hypothesis: If we cap a product sold by 10 or more identical sellers to a fixed-budget cash test with no brand build, then capital risk falls because heavy saturation is both a validation signal and a warning that it will not last as a durable brand.

signal.check: 10 or more accounts are found selling the identical item on the discovery platform, and the product is being planned as a long-term brand SKU.

expected_effect.size: 10 or more identical sellers signals a short-window cash test, not a brand

risk.note: One example in the source was a seasonal item; the cap applies broadly to any heavily copied product.

prerequisites: A competitor count of 10 or more identical sellers
steps: Count identical sellers on the discovery platform for the exact item.
If 10 or more, cap the plan to sample-quantity inventory and a fixed test budget.
Skip custom packaging and any brand-build spend for this product.
Judge the result honestly as a short cash opportunity, not a long-term product.

test.method: Track cash returned versus capital committed on capped cash-test products versus brand-build products

title: Treat a fragmented market with no leader as a possible opening, not proof
hypothesis: If we treat a fragmented market with no clear leader as a possible opening rather than confirmed proof, then fewer products are wrongly assumed easy to win because fragmentation alone does not confirm a gap.

signal.check: A candidate's market shows many small competitors with no dominant leader, and this is being read as an automatic opportunity.

expected_effect.size: unknown, hedged even by its own source

risk.note: A fragmented market can also mean the category itself is hard to win in, not just unclaimed.

prerequisites: A competitor scan showing no dominant leader
steps: Note the fragmentation as a possible opening, not confirmed proof.
Run the demand and margin checks as normal rather than skipping them on this signal alone.
Look for why no leader has emerged before assuming it is easy to become one.

test.method: Track hit rate of fragmented-market entries against the overall hit rate

title: Watch competitor density as an early sign a product's economics are shifting
hypothesis: If we track how a candidate's competitor count changes over the research and test window, then the team spots rising CPMs earlier because Meta is an auction and bidder scarcity is what produces outsized early results.

signal.check: A product's competitor count has not been re-checked since the initial screen, even though weeks have passed before the test launches.

risk.note: No source gives a specific multiplier for how much CPM rises per new bidder.

prerequisites: A candidate approaching its test launch date
steps: Re-check the exact-product competitor count right before launching the test, not just at initial screening.
Note any increase in bidders since the first screen.
Treat a rising bidder count as a signal the early-mover economics window may be closing.

test.method: Track CPM at launch against the competitor count change since initial screening

title: Skip a product recognized as long-running from repeated exposure
hypothesis: If we skip a product the researcher already recognizes from repeated exposure, then research time is spent on less-discovered candidates because familiarity itself is a saturation signal regardless of graph shape.
does_not_apply_when: A recognized product where a genuinely new, unserved angle has been found

signal.check: A candidate looks familiar from repeated exposure while screening, and no unserved angle has been identified for it yet.

risk.note: This conflicts with treating saturation as an opportunity when a real angle exists; use the angle audit to decide which applies.

prerequisites: A candidate spotted during scanning
steps: Note when a candidate feels recognizable from repeated exposure while scanning.
Treat that recall as a saturation signal and skip it by default.
Only revisit it if a genuinely new avatar or angle is later identified for it.

test.method: Track time saved per session by skipping recognized products versus researching them fully
test.read_point: at the end of each research session

title: Build a brand around a proven product and add secondary products before it fades
hypothesis: If we add evergreen secondary products around a proven hero once it validates, then revenue holds up longer because a winning product is not a moat and the hero's growth slows faster than a supporting range can be built.
does_not_apply_when: The hero product has not yet been proven in a live test

signal.check: The brand has one proven hero product and no named secondary or evergreen products in the pipeline.

expected_effect.size: one operator's secondary line grew about 20 percent a year while the hero declined faster

risk.note: Adding packaging or new SKUs too early, before proof, wastes cost and complexity.

prerequisites: A hero product with proven sales after its first test
steps: Confirm the hero product is proven before starting secondary product work.
List 2 to 3 evergreen products that extend the hero's function to adjacent needs.
Add branded packaging only now that the product is proven, as a defense against exact-offer copycats.
Set a trigger, such as first reorder or a revenue milestone, for launching each secondary product.

test.method: Track revenue share from secondary products against the hero product over time

title: List every angle competitors run, then name the avatar none of them serve
hypothesis: If we list every avatar and angle competitors already run and then name a genuine avatar none of them serve, then a saturated or served category still converts because the new angle answers an unmet need.
does_not_apply_when: The competitor count already graded green with no need for an angle

signal.check: The competition read came back amber or red, or the brand owns a product entering a category already well served, with no angle audit run yet.

risk.note: A forced avatar that does not genuinely fit the product wastes budget.

prerequisites: A competition read of amber or red, or an owned product entering a served category
steps: Catalogue the audiences and outcomes named in every competitor ad and page.
Write what customer type, life stage or outcome is missing from that list.
List 3 to 5 alternative avatars the product genuinely fits, and reject any forced fit.
Confirm each avatar has a real, provable reason the product serves them.

test.method: Test the new-avatar angle against a generic angle in a short ad set
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Prefer an angle that holds a small but real share of current ad volume
hypothesis: If we prefer an angle already holding a small nonzero share of current ad volume, then the pivot is less risky because some sellers have already proven that framing works, without it being fully saturated.

signal.check: A candidate angle's share of current ad volume in the category has not been estimated before choosing it.

expected_effect.size: about 10 percent of ads used the chosen framing in the source's example

risk.note: A literal 0 percent share is more opportunity but also more unproven-demand risk; the source does not resolve this trade-off.

prerequisites: A list of angles found during the ad library scan
steps: Count how many scanned ads use each candidate angle or framing.
Estimate each angle's share of total ad volume in the category.
Prefer an angle with a small but real share, such as around 10 percent.
Flag a 0 percent share as higher risk and higher opportunity, and note it as unproven.

test.method: Track hit rate of angles chosen at different share levels

title: Rebuild the whole page and creative around a new avatar, not bolt it on
hypothesis: If we rebuild the hook, page, imagery and proof entirely around a new avatar instead of adding it as a secondary message, then the pivot converts better because a bolted-on avatar dilutes the message for everyone.

signal.check: An angle pivot is planned that adds a new avatar's message as a secondary line on an existing page instead of rebuilding around it.

risk.note: None specific; this only changes how thoroughly the pivot is executed.

prerequisites: A chosen new avatar from the angle audit
steps: Keep the product and offer fixed when pivoting to a new avatar.
Rewrite the hook, page copy and imagery entirely around the new avatar's situation.
Rebuild the proof and testimonials to match the new avatar, not the old one.
Do not run the new avatar as a secondary line on the existing page.

test.method: Compare conversion rate of a fully rebuilt avatar page against a bolted-on version
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Build an offer structure as a differentiation lever instead of copying the product
hypothesis: If we build a distinct offer structure such as a named bundle, BOGO or a free gift threshold instead of copying the product itself, then the store differentiates from competitors without ever needing to copy anything they sell.

signal.check: The category's competitors mostly sell a bare listing with no bundle, BOGO or named offer structure.

expected_effect.size: AOV about 20 to 40 percent above base price via upsells, up to about 50 percent for a one-product store

risk.note: Any named ingredient or format claim inside the offer must be provable, never invented.

prerequisites: A margin gate that has already passed at the base price
steps: Check whether competitors run bare listings with no bundle or offer structure.
Design a named bundle, BOGO, free-gift threshold or multi-buy on top of the base product.
Re-run the margin gate at the offer's effective price, not the sticker price.
Confirm any named ingredient or claim inside the offer is provable before using it.

test.method: Track AOV before and after the offer structure launches
test.read_point: 30 days after the offer goes live

title: Use a branded or technical-sounding name only where the claim is provable
hypothesis: If we only use a branded or technical-sounding ingredient or format name when the underlying claim is provable, then perceived sophistication rises without any risk of an invented efficacy claim.

signal.check: A technical or branded-sounding name for an ingredient or format is being considered for the product angle.

risk.note: Any claim behind the name must be provable; do not invent efficacy to sound more sophisticated.

prerequisites: A specific ingredient, format or mechanism the product actually uses
steps: Identify the real, provable ingredient, format or mechanism behind the product.
Check whether a more technical or specific name for it exists and is accurate.
Confirm the brand can back the claim if a buyer asks or a regulator checks.
Use the technical name in copy only where it is accurate.

test.method: A/B test the technical name against the plain description on the PDP
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Change exactly one variable from the category's core expectation
hypothesis: If we change exactly one major variable from what buyers expect in the category instead of several, then the product reads as a clear, understandable innovation because too many changes at once make it look unfamiliar and risky.

signal.check: A new product concept changes 2 or more major variables from the category's norm at once, such as shape, color, format and benefit framing together.

expected_effect.size: unknown, framed as a design principle, not a measured lift

risk.note: A product design change is harder to undo once tooling or packaging is committed.

prerequisites: A concept with more than one deviation from the category norm
steps: List every way the new concept differs from the category's standard expectation.
Pick the single sharpest, most defensible contrast to keep.
Revert every other listed deviation back to the familiar category norm.
Park the other ideas as future line extensions, not part of this launch.

test.method: Compare buyer reaction and conversion on the single-variable concept against a multi-variable version in concept testing
test.read_point: before committing to tooling or packaging

title: Borrow design and mechanics from a distant industry, not a competitor
hypothesis: If we borrow shape, mechanism or ritual ideas from an industry far outside the category instead of copying a direct competitor, then the product reads as original because the further apart the source and the category, the more powerful the idea feels.

signal.check: A design or mechanic idea for the product was borrowed directly from a competitor in the same category instead of a distant industry.

expected_effect.size: unknown, failure risk rises with distance per the source's own caveat

risk.note: The source itself notes failure risk rises the further the borrowed idea is from the category.

prerequisites: A design or mechanic problem to solve for the product
steps: List industries with no obvious connection to the category.
Look at their shapes, mechanisms and rituals for something transferable.
Sketch how the borrowed idea could apply to this product without copying a direct competitor.
Test the concept with the qualitative pass before committing to tooling.

test.method: Run the borrowed-design concept through the qualitative concept pass and compare reaction to a conventional design

title: Name a self-interested and a feel-good reason to buy for every product
hypothesis: If we write both a self-interested reason and a feel-good reason to buy for every product, then conversion and repeat purchase rise because buyers respond to both benefit and identity, not benefit alone.

signal.check: The product's messaging states only a functional benefit, with no feel-good or identity-level reason to buy alongside it.

risk.note: Any claim used in either reason must be provable, per the no-invented-claims rule.

prerequisites: A confirmed core benefit for the product
steps: Write the self-interested reason to buy in one sentence, such as a functional or health benefit.
Write the feel-good reason to buy in one sentence, such as an identity or values-based benefit.
Check any claim inside both reasons against country-specific claim rules before using it.
Use both reasons together in PDP copy and creative hooks.

test.method: A/B a page with both reasons stated against a page with only the functional reason
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Classify every candidate evergreen or trending before spending
hypothesis: If we classify every candidate as evergreen or trending before spending and match budget and patience to the class, then capital is protected because a trending pick is treated as fast cash, not a brand-build bet.

signal.check: A candidate has not been classified evergreen or trending before its budget and inventory plan were set.

expected_effect.size: trending gives fast cash and is gone in about 2 to 4 weeks; evergreen starts slower but can carry a brand for years

risk.note: A brand holding inventory should default to evergreen unless it can exit a trending pick fast.

prerequisites: A validated candidate approaching the budget and inventory decision
steps: Classify the candidate market as growing, flat, fad or declining.
Label the product evergreen or trending based on that classification.
For a trending pick, cap the plan to sample-quantity inventory, a fixed test budget and no custom packaging.
For an evergreen pick, run the full validation and launch stack.

test.method: Track capital at risk and cash recovered on evergreen versus trending launches
test.read_point: end of each product's test window

title: Map seasonality across several years and plan cash around it
hypothesis: If we map a product's seasonality across several years before launch, then cash flow is protected because recurring spikes concentrate both revenue and risk in predictable windows.

signal.check: A candidate's seasonality has not been mapped across multiple years before inventory or cash planning.

expected_effect.size: one operator made about 80 percent of profit across 2 holiday months

risk.note: Extreme seasonal concentration raises cash flow risk even when total annual revenue looks healthy.

prerequisites: A multi-year trend view for the candidate
steps: Plot the trend tool's monthly data across several years for the candidate.
Mark recurring monthly spikes, such as a holiday, and note their size relative to the rest of the year.
Plan cash and inventory timing around the spike months, not an even monthly assumption.
For gifting or occasion-driven spikes, apply the same cash and inventory plan as a holiday spike.

test.method: Track cash position through the identified spike and off-peak months

title: Never commit MOQ inventory against a trend spike with no history
hypothesis: If we refuse to place an MOQ inventory order against a product with a steep, historyless trend spike, then inventory write-offs fall because a no-history spike can collapse before the order even arrives.

signal.check: An MOQ inventory order is being considered for a product whose demand spike has no multi-month history behind it.

risk.note: An MOQ order placed against a spike cannot be undone if the spike collapses before it sells through.

prerequisites: A trend spike candidate under consideration for an MOQ order
steps: Check the candidate's 180-day or multi-month trend history before ordering inventory.
If the spike has no prior history, treat it as a gamble, not a validated winner.
Cap the order to a sample or small trial batch instead of a full MOQ.
Only place a full MOQ order once the trend shows a sustained pattern, not a single spike.

test.method: Track sell-through and write-off rate on MOQ orders placed with versus without multi-month trend history

title: Map gifting and occasion spikes the same way as holiday seasonality
hypothesis: If we map festival, wedding season and gifting-occasion demand with the same cash and inventory plan used for major holidays, then cash flow risk falls because occasion-driven spikes concentrate revenue just as sharply as Christmas or Black Friday.

signal.check: A candidate spikes mainly around a gifting or cultural occasion, and no cash or inventory plan has been made for that specific window.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: Occasion dates shift year to year in some calendars and must be re-checked each planning cycle.

prerequisites: A candidate with an identified gifting or occasion demand pattern
steps: Identify which festivals, wedding seasons or gifting occasions drive the candidate's demand.
Mark those dates on the same cash and inventory calendar used for Black Friday or Christmas.
Plan stock arrival and cash reserves to land before the occasion window, not during it.
Re-check occasion dates each year since some shift on a lunar or regional calendar.

test.method: Track stockout days and cash position through the occasion window
test.read_point: the week after the occasion window closes

title: Check real replenishment rate before assuming a subscription model
hypothesis: If we check a product's real usage-based replenishment rate before assuming it supports a subscription, then subscription churn falls because the cadence actually matches how often the product runs out.
does_not_apply_when: A durable or rarely-repurchased product being pitched as a monthly subscription

signal.check: A subscription plan is being built for a product without checking how often a real buyer actually uses up or replaces a unit.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one product example: 33 percent subscribed and over 5000 dollars a month recurring; one store had 0 subscribers

risk.note: Subscription fit is optional, not guaranteed, even for a consumable product.

prerequisites: Real or estimated usage frequency data for the product
steps: Estimate how often a typical buyer uses up or needs to replace one unit.
Compare that cadence to the proposed subscription interval.
If the product is used only a couple of times a year, do not pitch a monthly subscription.
Set the subscription interval to match the real replenishment rate if one is offered at all.

test.method: Track subscription churn and skip rate against the assumed replenishment interval

title: Reject novelty products with no real recurring value
hypothesis: If we reject viral novelty products with no real recurring value, then refund and return rates stay lower because true winners relieve a pain, hygiene, fitness or convenience problem a buyer would use again a month later.

signal.check: A candidate is a novelty item riding a viral moment with no clear ongoing use case a month after purchase.

risk.note: None; this only screens out a category of weak candidates before spend.

prerequisites: A candidate under consideration from organic or viral scouting
steps: Ask whether the buyer would still use the product a month after purchase.
Check it relieves a real pain, hygiene, fitness or convenience problem, not just novelty appeal.
Drop the candidate if the honest answer is no.
