test.method: Track return and refund rate on novelty-screened products versus ones that skipped this check

title: Judge whether a novelty creates repeat purchase or is a one-time sale
hypothesis: If we explicitly judge whether a format innovation creates a repeat-purchase annuity or is a durable one-time purchase, then the revenue plan is realistic because a durable novelty item will not generate consumable-style repeat orders.

signal.check: A format innovation on a commodity product has not been judged as either a repeat-purchase annuity or a durable one-time buy.

risk.note: None; this only sets a realistic revenue-model expectation.

prerequisites: A format-innovation candidate on an existing commodity
steps: Ask whether the product wears out, gets used up or needs replacing.
If it is durable, plan the revenue model as one-time purchase with cross-sell, not repeat purchase.
If it is consumable, plan for repeat purchase and possibly subscription.

test.method: Track actual repeat purchase rate against the planned revenue model classification

title: Weight lifetime value, not just AOV, for a low-ticket repeat item
hypothesis: If we weight lifetime value instead of only AOV when a product's repeat-purchase potential is strong, then a low-AOV item can still clear the margin gate because repeat orders make up for a thin single-order margin.
does_not_apply_when: A product with unclear or unproven repeat usage

signal.check: A low-AOV candidate is being rejected on the margin gate using single-order economics alone, without checking its repeat-purchase potential.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: Projected LTV is a forecast, not a guarantee, until real repeat data exists for the product.

prerequisites: Some evidence or a reasonable estimate of repeat usage frequency
steps: Estimate expected repeat purchase frequency and average order count over 180 days.
Calculate projected lifetime value at that repeat rate.
Re-run the margin gate using LTV instead of single-order margin for this candidate.
Mark the memo provisional until real repeat data replaces the estimate.

test.method: Track real repeat rate and LTV against the projected figures after launch

title: Reject a product priced too low to cover paid-acquisition cost
hypothesis: If we reject a candidate priced at about 9.99 dollars or below on the source platform, then paid-acquisition tests are not wasted on products with no room to cover Meta or TikTok acquisition cost.
does_not_apply_when: A deliberate low-ticket lead product with a defined upsell path to recover margin

signal.check: A candidate's source-platform or planned retail price is at or below about 9.99 dollars with no offer structure to raise the effective order value.

expected_effect.size: reject at about 9.99 dollars or below

risk.note: A deliberate low-ticket lead-product strategy is a valid exception if the upsell path is planned and tested.

prerequisites: A source or planned retail price for the candidate
steps: Check the candidate's price on the source platform or its planned retail price.
Reject candidates at about 9.99 dollars or below unless an upsell path is explicitly planned.
If used as a lead product, model the full funnel margin, not just the entry price.

test.method: Track CPA and contribution margin on sub-10-dollar products against the brand's other price points
test.read_point: after each product's short paid test

title: Target a mid-range retail price band for a paid-acquisition launch
hypothesis: If we target a retail price in the 50 to 150 dollar band for a paid-acquisition launch instead of a lower price, then margin per order is more likely to cover acquisition cost because the band leaves room to pay for a paid test.
does_not_apply_when: luxury_considered

signal.check: A candidate's planned retail price sits in the 9 to 20 dollar caution range or has not been checked against the target band at all.

expected_effect.size: target band 50 to 150 dollars, caution at 9 to 20 dollars

risk.note: The band is described as accepted practice by the source with no independent data behind it.

prerequisites: A price set from comparable products
steps: Set the price using roughly 2 dozen comparable products, not just one competitor.
Check whether the price sits in the 50 to 150 dollar target band.
For a price in the 9 to 20 dollar caution range, treat it as a red flag needing a strong branding or AOV plan to offset it.
For a luxury or considered-purchase store, raise the band and rely less on this default.

test.method: Track gross margin per order and CPA-covering rate at the chosen price against the target band

title: Gate every candidate on a dollar margin floor and a price to cost multiple together
hypothesis: If we require a candidate to pass both a minimum dollar gross margin and a minimum price-to-landed-cost multiple at the same time, then fewer unprofitable products reach a paid test because the dollar floor catches low-cost items the multiple alone would pass.

signal.check: A candidate has only been checked against one margin rule, either the dollar floor or the multiple, not both together.

expected_effect.size: at least 30 dollars a unit and at least 3 times landed cost, both together, 40 dollars preferred

risk.note: These dollar and multiple figures are placeholders from the source until the brand's own contribution target replaces them.

prerequisites: A landed cost and a planned retail price for the candidate
steps: Calculate gross margin as price minus landed cost.
Check gate 1: gross margin at least 30 dollars, 40 preferred.
Check gate 2: price at least 3 times landed cost.
Fail the candidate if either gate fails, even if the other passes.

test.method: Track actual net margin after ads on products that passed both gates versus only one

title: Model markup at the low end, high end and future bulk cost of the price range
hypothesis: If we model markup at the low end, high end and future bulk cost of the realistic price range instead of one point, then pricing decisions are more robust because a margin that only works at the top of the range is fragile.

signal.check: A margin calculation has been run at only one price point, not the low end, high end and expected bulk cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one example: 583 dollars per 100 units was a concern at 9 dollars and healthy at 20 dollars

risk.note: A supplier's bulk-tier quote is not guaranteed to arrive automatically; always ask for a re-quote.

prerequisites: A price range and a first-order and bulk supplier quote
steps: Calculate margin at the low end of the realistic retail price range.
Calculate margin at the high end of the range.
Calculate margin again using the expected bulk-order landed cost.
If only the high end of the range or the bulk cost passes, verify buyers will actually pay that price before sourcing.

test.method: Track actual margin achieved at the launch price against the low, high and bulk projections

title: Re-quote your own supplier cost instead of assuming a competitor's
hypothesis: If we get our own supplier quote instead of assuming a competitor's cost base, then the margin gate reflects reality because an established competitor has usually negotiated a better rate a new seller cannot match.

signal.check: A margin calculation is using an estimated or competitor-implied cost instead of the brand's own supplier quote.

risk.note: None; this only replaces an assumption with a real quote.

prerequisites: A candidate supplier willing to quote
steps: Get a direct quote from a real supplier at the planned order quantity.
Do not assume the brand can match a competitor's implied or estimated cost.
Use the brand's own quote in every margin calculation from this point forward.

test.method: Compare the assumed competitor-based cost against the brand's own confirmed quote
test.read_point: once the first real quote is in hand

title: Set price from a broad set of comparable products, not one competitor
hypothesis: If we set price from about 2 dozen comparable products instead of one competitor, then pricing is more defensible because a single reference point can be an outlier in either direction.

signal.check: A launch price was set by matching or slightly undercutting a single competitor, without a broader comparable set.

risk.note: One operator's heuristic count, not a measured optimum.

prerequisites: Access to search results or marketplace listings for the category
steps: Pull prices from about 2 dozen comparable products in the category and adjacent formats.
Note the range and the median price point.
Set the launch price using that range, not a single competitor's price.
Re-check the price against the margin gate at this level.

test.method: Compare conversion and margin at the broadly-set price against a single-competitor-matched price
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Separate a fixable execution problem from a structural cost problem
hypothesis: If we separate a fixable operational problem from a structural cost problem before scaling ad spend on early signal, then wasted spend falls because ad spend cannot fix input costs outside the brand's control.

signal.check: Early signal on a candidate is strong but margin is thin, and the team has not diagnosed whether the cause is fixable copy and pricing or a structural cost the brand cannot control.

risk.note: Continuing to fund a structurally uneconomic category burns capital that a fixable-copy problem would not.

prerequisites: A candidate with strong qualitative signal but weak margin
steps: List every input cost driving the weak margin: raw materials, shipping, fees, leases, capital requirements.
Check which of those the brand can actually change through negotiation, volume or sourcing.
Separately list execution issues: weak copy, a mispriced offer, a slow page.
Scale spend only on the fixable execution issues; stop the category if the cost problem is structural.

test.method: Track margin recovery after fixing execution issues on a strong-signal, thin-margin candidate
test.read_point: after the fix is implemented and retested

title: Price payment-gateway friction into the margin gate
hypothesis: If we price COD collection fees, failed-payment retry cost and prepaid-discount cost into the margin gate, then the contribution margin figure is accurate because payment-gateway friction is a real cost the gross margin check ignores.

signal.check: The margin gate uses gross margin only and does not include COD collection fees, failed-payment retries or prepaid discount costs.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: COD and payment-retry costs vary a lot by market and payment provider and must be measured, not assumed.

prerequisites: Payment processor and COD collection fee data from the brand's own history
steps: Pull the brand's COD collection fee rate, if COD is offered.
Pull the failed-payment retry cost rate from the payment processor.
Pull the cost of any prepaid-order discount offered to steer away from COD.
Add all 3 into the contribution margin calculation in the unit economics gate.

test.method: Compare projected contribution margin including payment friction against actual realized margin

title: Price real shipping cost before sourcing a heavy or oversized item
hypothesis: If we price a real shipment on the carrier's site before sourcing a heavy or oversized item, then margin is protected because shipping can eat a large share of the cost-to-price spread on bulky products.

signal.check: A candidate is heavy or oversized and its shipping cost has not been priced on an actual carrier rate page.

risk.note: For a pure dropshipping model, a hard skip is the simpler and safer default for heavy items.

prerequisites: Estimated packed size and weight for the candidate
steps: Estimate the packed size and weight of the product.
Price a real shipment on the actual carrier's website, not an assumed flat rate.
Calculate shipping as a share of the price-to-cost spread.
Reject or reprice the candidate if shipping eats a large share of that spread.

test.method: Compare projected shipping cost against actual outbound shipping cost after launch

title: Choose materials and packaging that survive parcel handling
hypothesis: If we choose materials and packaging that survive parcel handling, such as plastic over glass, then refund and return rates fall because breakage in transit is a margin and reputation cost that is fully avoidable.

signal.check: The candidate's packaging or material choice has not been tested for transit survival, or uses a fragile material like glass.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one venture's glass vials broke in shipping and killed the product line

risk.note: Switching material after a failed transit test can mean re-tooling packaging.

prerequisites: A sample unit and its planned shipping packaging
steps: Choose durable, transit-friendly materials such as plastic over glass where possible.
Ship a real sample through the intended parcel network and inspect on arrival.
If breakage occurs, change the material or add protective packaging before ordering inventory.
Log the transit test result with the supplier brief.

test.method: Track transit damage rate and related refund rate after launch

title: Require shelf life to comfortably outlast the time to market and sell
hypothesis: If we require shelf life to comfortably exceed the realistic time to build marketing and sell through inventory, then write-offs fall because a perishable or degradable product with a short shelf life can expire before it reaches most buyers.
does_not_apply_when: A non-perishable, non-degradable product

signal.check: A perishable or degradable candidate's shelf life has not been compared against the realistic time to market and sell through inventory.

expected_effect.size: one example judged about 3 years as more than enough

risk.note: None; this only prevents ordering a batch that could expire before selling through.

prerequisites: A shelf life figure from the supplier
steps: Get the confirmed shelf life from the supplier, not an assumed figure.
Estimate realistic time to build marketing plus expected sell-through time for the first order.
Add the customer's own time to use a unit after purchase.
Reject or shorten the order size if shelf life is shorter than that combined ramp.

test.method: Track units expired or written off against the shelf life margin planned at sourcing
test.read_point: at the shelf life expiry date of the first order

title: Check claim, labeling and registration rules per country before any spend
hypothesis: If we research claim, labeling and registration rules for every target country before any ad or sourcing spend, then no SKU is voided after money has already gone into samples or ads.

signal.check: A candidate in a regulated category, such as food, cosmetics, supplements or baby products, has not had its per-country claim and labeling rules checked.

risk.note: A regulatory miss after launch can force a full product or claim recall, an unrecoverable cost.

prerequisites: A defined target country list for the candidate
steps: Identify whether the category needs specific claim, labeling, packaging or testing documentation.
Research the current rules per target country before any spend, especially for food, cosmetics, supplements and baby products.
Check registration, sizing standards, returns and payment rules for any new country.
Treat any red flag here as a hard stop until resolved, with no override allowed.

test.method: Track regulatory-related incidents or takedowns after launch against the pre-launch check

title: Check delivery window targets and their effect on chargebacks
hypothesis: If we check the candidate's realistic delivery window against a 6 to 10 day target and its effect on refunds and chargebacks, then payout risk falls because slower delivery windows measurably raise dispute rates.

signal.check: A candidate's expected delivery time has not been checked against the 6 to 10 day target window or the brand's own measured delivery data.

expected_effect.size: 6 to 10 days target, 8 to 15 acceptable early, 10 to 15 or more raises chargebacks

risk.note: A faster shipping line can add real cost per unit; only worth it if AOV absorbs the difference.

prerequisites: A shipping line quote or the brand's own 3PL delivery data
steps: Get the expected delivery time for the target country from the supplier or 3PL.
Compare it against a 6 to 10 day target, or the brand's own measured delivery days and refund rate if available.
If delivery runs 10 to 15 days or more, budget for higher chargeback and refund handling.
Consider a faster shipping line only if the added cost per unit is absorbed by AOV.

test.method: Track refund and chargeback rate against actual measured delivery days per country
test.read_point: first 90 days after launch in that country

title: Check trademark and licensing exposure before listing a fandom-adjacent product
hypothesis: If we check trademark and licensing exposure before listing any fandom-adjacent or licensed-look product, then a launch is not lost to a takedown after ad spend and inventory are already committed.
does_not_apply_when: The product has no character, brand or design element resembling a licensed or fandom property

signal.check: A candidate uses a character, design or branding element that resembles a licensed or fandom property, with no trademark check done yet.

risk.note: A takedown after launch costs the ad spend and the SKU, and can carry legal liability.

prerequisites: A candidate with any fandom-adjacent or licensed-look design element
steps: List every character, brand name or design element in the product that could resemble a licensed property.
Check trademark and licensing status for each one before any listing or ad spend.
Drop or redesign any element that carries real exposure.
Treat this check with the same hard-stop rigor as the country regulatory check.

test.method: Track whether any launched product later receives a takedown or legal notice

title: Price return-to-origin and COD collection cost for a mobile-first COD market
hypothesis: If we price the return-to-origin rate and COD collection cost into the margin gate for a mobile-first, cash-on-delivery market, then fewer products fail after launch because a high RTO rate can erase margin even after every other check passes.
does_not_apply_when: A market with no cash-on-delivery option

signal.check: A candidate targets a cash-on-delivery-heavy market and its return-to-origin rate has not been priced into the margin gate.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: RTO rates vary sharply by category, price point and courier, so a generic assumption can be badly wrong.

prerequisites: The brand's or category's historical RTO rate for cash-on-delivery orders
steps: Pull the brand's own RTO rate for COD orders, or a reasonable category estimate if the brand is new to COD.
Estimate the cost of a returned, undelivered order: return shipping, restocking and lost sale.
Add the COD collection fee charged by the courier or payment partner.
Re-run the margin gate including these costs before launch in a COD-heavy market.

test.method: Track actual RTO rate and its margin impact after launch

title: Check for a category-specific certification beyond general regulatory clearance
hypothesis: If we check for a category-specific certification such as hallmarking, a safety mark or ingredient clearance beyond the general regulatory check, then the product avoids a compliance block that a generic country check would miss.
does_not_apply_when: A category with no known certification requirement beyond general labeling rules

signal.check: A candidate is in a category known to need a specific certification, such as jewelry, electronics, toys or cosmetics, and only the general regulatory check has been run.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one example cites GreenGuard Gold on a crib product with no general method given

risk.note: Missing a required certification can block import or sale entirely in the target country.

prerequisites: A candidate in a category with known certification requirements
steps: Identify the candidate's category-specific certification needs: hallmarking for jewelry, a safety mark for electronics or toys, ingredient clearance for cosmetics.
Confirm with the supplier whether the product already holds that certification.
Verify the certification is valid and current for the target country.
Treat a missing required certification as a hard stop until resolved.

test.method: Track whether any launched product is blocked or flagged for a missing certification

title: Launch with exactly one SKU and add variants only after proof
hypothesis: If we launch with exactly one SKU and treat variants as complexity debt to add later, then inventory capital and shipping mix-ups fall because fewer sizes, colors and formulations mean less to manage before proof exists.
does_not_apply_when: A catalogue brand adding to an existing proven range, or a hero product already proven

signal.check: A first launch plan includes multiple variants, sizes or formulations before the core product has sold.

risk.note: Once demand is proven, add a range and evergreen secondary products, per the SKU-count conflict resolution.

prerequisites: A candidate approaching its first launch plan
steps: Cut the launch plan down to exactly 1 SKU, 1 size, 1 formulation.
Park every variant idea for after the first proof of sales.
Set the trigger for adding a range: first reorder or a set revenue milestone.
Add evergreen secondary products and AOV-boosting upsells only after that trigger.

test.method: Track inventory turns and stock mix-up incidents on single-SKU launches versus multi-variant launches

title: Reverse-image search a competitor's photo to find the supplier cost floor
hypothesis: If we reverse-image search a competitor's product photo, then the real supplier cost floor is found faster because the same or a similar listing usually surfaces on a wholesale marketplace.

signal.check: A candidate's cost floor has not been checked by reverse-image searching a competitor's product photo.

expected_effect.size: unknown, examples show large cost floors relative to competitor retail price

risk.note: The listing found may differ in quality and spec from the competitor's actual unit, so this finds a cost floor, not a final quote.

prerequisites: A competitor's product photo to search
steps: Right-click the competitor's product photo from their ad or page and run a reverse image search.
Scroll to a matching listing on a wholesale marketplace.
Record the listing price, MOQ, variants and shipping options.
Note where the listing's spec may differ from the competitor's actual unit before treating this as a final cost.

test.method: Compare the reverse-image cost floor against the final negotiated supplier quote
test.read_point: once the real supplier quote is in hand

title: Write one structured sourcing request with MOQ, certifications and review strength
hypothesis: If we write one structured sourcing request naming OEM service, an MOQ ceiling, certifications and review strength, then supplier shortlisting is faster and more comparable because every response answers the same defined criteria.

signal.check: Supplier outreach is being done with an unstructured, ad hoc message instead of one repeatable structured request.

risk.note: None; this only standardizes an existing outreach step.

prerequisites: A defined product spec and a funded MOQ ceiling
steps: Write a request naming OEM service or private label, an MOQ ceiling the brand can fund, required certifications and expected review strength.
Send the same request to every candidate supplier for comparability.
Score each response on wholesale cost, target retail, MOQ range, margin, reorder rate and stated match reason.
Separate suppliers who match the product requirement from ones who only match the general category.

test.method: Track time to a comparable, complete supplier shortlist using the structured request versus ad hoc outreach

title: Translate consumer language into manufacturing specification before contacting suppliers
hypothesis: If we translate consumer-facing language into precise manufacturing terms before contacting suppliers, then quotes come back more accurate because vague consumer adjectives invite inflated or mismatched quotes.

signal.check: An RFQ or supplier message uses consumer adjectives such as quiet or matte instead of manufacturing specification terms.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one operator's opinion on supplier psychology, not independently tested

risk.note: This is one operator's opinion, not a tested result.

prerequisites: A draft RFQ using consumer-facing language
steps: List every consumer-facing feature description in the draft RFQ.
Translate each into a manufacturing term, such as quiet keyboard into a 5-layer internal dampening structure, or matte paint into e-coating.
Send the translated, specific RFQ to suppliers instead of the consumer-language version.

test.method: Compare quote accuracy and revision count between translated and untranslated RFQs

title: Vet a shortlisted supplier with specific capability questions by phone
hypothesis: If we vet a shortlisted supplier with 2 to 3 specific capability questions by phone regardless of their platform rating, then poor-fit suppliers are caught before a sample order because a high rating is not proof of a good experience.

signal.check: A supplier is being selected mainly on platform rating, with no direct phone call about product-specific capability.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a 4.7 rating alone is called explicitly not proof of a good experience

risk.note: A vague or dodged answer is a stronger signal than the platform rating.

prerequisites: A shortlisted supplier with a listed rating
steps: Write 2 to 3 specific capability questions tied to the product's differentiation.
Call the shortlisted supplier directly and ask the questions.
Rate the answers specific or vague.
Drop a supplier who gives vague answers, even with a high platform rating.

test.method: Track sample and order quality outcomes for suppliers vetted this way versus rating-only selection
test.read_point: after the first sample is received

title: Order a small sample through your own fulfillment chain before an MOQ order
hypothesis: If we order a small sample through the store's own fulfillment chain before committing to MOQ inventory, then a failing sample kills the SKU before a large cash commitment instead of after.
does_not_apply_when: A resale model with no ability to control which unit reaches the customer for testing

signal.check: An MOQ order is planned before a sample has been received and tested through the store's own fulfillment chain, not only the factory.

expected_effect.size: 1 sample first, then about 50 units for a first production run, never thousands

risk.note: Skipping this step and going straight to a large MOQ risks the full order failing on unboxing, shelf life or fit.

prerequisites: A shortlisted, phone-vetted supplier
steps: Order 1 sample and have it shipped through the store's own fulfillment chain, not only received directly from the factory.
Test the sample for durability, packaging survival and whether it can be demoed on camera.
Order about 50 units for a first production run once the sample passes.
Never commit to a multi-thousand-unit order before this stage clears.

test.method: Track how many samples fail this stage versus how many later-stage MOQ problems occur when it is skipped

title: Compare a private sourcing agent against marketplace-direct ordering on real numbers
hypothesis: If we compare a private sourcing agent's quote and delivery days against marketplace-direct ordering for a no-inventory store, then the cheaper, faster channel is chosen on real numbers instead of the channel with the most affiliate promotion.
does_not_apply_when: A store that holds its own stock and sources through private-label manufacturing

signal.check: A sourcing channel has been chosen because it was recommended, without comparing cost, speed and branding options against at least one alternative.

risk.note: Every promoted sourcing platform in the source material has a commercial interest in being recommended; verify pricing and terms independently.

prerequisites: A no-inventory store considering a sourcing channel
steps: Get a quote and delivery estimate from a private sourcing agent, including branded packaging options.
Get a quote and delivery estimate from a marketplace-direct channel for the same product.
Compare cost, delivery days, branding options and support responsiveness between the two.
Check whether the person recommending either channel has a referral or affiliate interest in it.

test.method: Track measured delivery days, sample quality and total landed cost by sourcing channel chosen
test.read_point: after the first order through the chosen channel

title: Add custom branding and packaging only after the product is proven to sell
hypothesis: If we add custom logo, mailer and packaging only after the product is proven to sell, then wasted spend on unproven SKUs falls because branding cost and complexity are deferred until there is something worth defending.

signal.check: Custom packaging or branded mailers are being ordered for a product that has not yet had a proven sales test.

risk.note: For a brand where packaging is core to the product concept, stage sample-run packaging for the test and full custom packaging after the first reorder.

prerequisites: A candidate that has not yet completed its first sales test
steps: Use generic or minimal packaging for the first sample-quantity test.
Wait for the product to clear its first proven sales test before ordering custom packaging.
For a brand where packaging is part of the product concept, stage a small custom run at test size, then full custom packaging after the first reorder.

test.method: Track spend on packaging and mailers before versus after proof, and whether any pre-proof spend was wasted
test.read_point: after the first sales test concludes

title: Set a reminder to re-quote every supplier as order volume grows
hypothesis: If we set a reminder to re-quote every supplier as order volume crosses a threshold, then the margin gate stays accurate because landed cost at 1 unit tier can be very different at 500 or 1000 units.

signal.check: A product's margin is still using its original first-order quote even though order volume has crossed 500 or 1000 units.

expected_effect.size: re-quote thresholds at about 500 and 1000 units

risk.note: None; this only adds a calendar check.

prerequisites: A product with an existing supplier and a growing order volume
steps: Set a calendar reminder tied to order volume thresholds, such as 500 and 1000 units.
Ask the supplier for a re-quote at the current volume tier when the threshold is hit.
Update the margin gate with the new landed cost figure.
Do not assume the original quote still holds as volume scales.

test.method: Track landed cost changes captured through re-quotes against margin assumptions

title: Verify an AI-surfaced supplier is actually reachable on the named platform
hypothesis: If we verify an AI-surfaced supplier is actually reachable on the platform it names, then wasted outreach falls because AI shortlists can name a supplier that is not actually listed where claimed.

signal.check: A supplier shortlist came from an AI agent and has not been checked for whether each supplier is actually reachable on the named platform.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one demo's first shortlist was not on the platform until a follow-up prompt verified it

risk.note: None; this only adds a required verification step before outreach.

prerequisites: An AI-generated supplier shortlist
steps: Take each AI-suggested supplier name and platform claim.
Search the named platform directly to confirm the supplier is actually listed there.
Ask the AI agent to re-verify reachability with a follow-up prompt if any are missing.
Only contact suppliers confirmed reachable on the named platform.

test.method: Track what share of AI-suggested suppliers are confirmed reachable on first check

title: Price warranty and after-sales cost for a considered-purchase category
hypothesis: If we price warranty and after-sales support cost into the supplier brief for a considered-purchase category, then the margin gate reflects reality because a low landed cost can still fail once return and repair handling are added.
does_not_apply_when: A low-ticket, impulse-purchase category with no expected warranty claims

signal.check: A candidate in electronics, jewelry or appliances has a margin gate that does not include warranty or repair handling cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no general method given, verify against brand data

risk.note: Warranty claim rates are hard to estimate before launch and should be revised as real data comes in.

prerequisites: A considered-purchase candidate approaching the supplier brief stage
steps: Estimate expected warranty claim rate for the category from industry norms or the supplier's own data.
Estimate the cost per warranty claim: replacement, repair or refund handling.
Add expected after-sales support cost per order to the contribution margin calculation.
Re-check the margin gate with these costs included before sourcing.

test.method: Track actual warranty claim rate and cost against the pre-launch estimate

title: Keep a research log with a fixed set of columns for every candidate
hypothesis: If we keep a single research log with a fixed column set for every candidate, then decisions become auditable and comparable because every candidate carries the same evidence trail regardless of who researched it.

signal.check: Candidates are being tracked in scattered notes or memory instead of one structured log with consistent columns.

risk.note: None; this is a process change with no downside.

prerequisites: A shared spreadsheet or tool for the research log
steps: Create one sheet with columns: date, product, source method, buy price, sell price, gross margin, demand read, competitor count and color, revenue estimate, angle status, evergreen or trending, notes.
Log every candidate as it is found, not only the ones that get funded.
Record every rule override with the overriding signal in the same log.
Review the log weekly to narrow to the strongest candidates for deeper validation.

test.method: Track how many candidates have a complete row versus missing fields over time

title: Stop product research at a validated product and hand off the rest
hypothesis: If product research work stops at a validated product with evidence attached instead of continuing into creative or media work, then each workstream moves faster because it has a clear, separately owned handoff point.

signal.check: The same person or process is trying to both validate the product and build creative or media for it, with no clear handoff point.

risk.note: None; this only clarifies ownership boundaries.

prerequisites: A validated product with a completed memo
steps: Confirm the go or no-go decision and validation memo are complete for the product.
Hand the angle brief to the creative owner, the test brief to the media owner, and the supplier brief to the operations owner.
Stop product research involvement once handoffs are made, unless a post-test diagnosis is needed.

test.method: Track time from validated product to first live test across products with a clean handoff versus without

title: Score candidate expansion markets instead of copying another brand's country order
hypothesis: If we score each candidate expansion market on competitor count, delivery cost, compliance and localization cost instead of copying a fixed country order from another brand's case study, then the next market is chosen on the store's own numbers, not someone else's history.
does_not_apply_when: The product has not yet proven demand and economics in at least 1 market

signal.check: A next-market decision is being made by copying another brand's stated expansion order instead of scoring markets on the brand's own numbers.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source gives a metric for when a market is proven enough to move on

risk.note: No source gives a firm metric for proven enough to expand; set the brand's own placeholder and revise it.

prerequisites: Product-market fit proven in at least 1 market
steps: List candidate next markets rather than assuming a fixed sequence.
Score each on exact-product competitor count, delivery days and cost, duty and VAT, and localization cost.
Enter the cheapest-to-win market next, whichever it is.
Set the brand's own proven enough to expand metric, such as a CPA bar held for 4 consecutive weeks.

test.method: Track CPA and time to profitability in each new market against its pre-entry score
test.read_point: 4 weeks after entering each new market

title: Localize creative and re-check duty and VAT before entering a new country
hypothesis: If we localize creative and re-check duty, VAT, shipping time and sizing before entering a new country, then margin holds because these costs can erase the advantage that looked good on paper.

signal.check: A new country is being entered with creative and pricing copied from the home market, without checking local duty, VAT, shipping time and sizing.

risk.note: Duty, VAT and compliance rules can change without notice and must be re-checked close to entry.

prerequisites: A chosen next market from the expansion scoring
steps: Localize ad and page creative for the new market's language and cultural context.
Check current duty and VAT rates for the product category in that country.
Confirm shipping time, sizing standards and any registration requirement.
Re-run the margin gate with these country-specific costs before spend.

test.method: Track realized margin in the new country against the pre-entry projection

title: Use founder excitement only as a tiebreaker between equally validated concepts
hypothesis: If we use founder and team excitement only as a tiebreaker between concepts that already passed the demand and economics checks equally, then decisions stay evidence-led while still using a real signal for founder-driven execution energy.
does_not_apply_when: A single concept with no equally-validated alternative to compare it against

signal.check: Founder excitement is being used to choose the concept before the demand and economics checks have run, instead of after they run and tie.

risk.note: This is an input to the decision, never a replacement for the data-led validation stack.

prerequisites: 2 or 3 concept directions that passed the validation stack equally
steps: Run each concept through the full demand and economics checks first.
Only for concepts that tie or are close, ask which direction the team is most excited by.
Show the finalists to friends, family or trusted advisors for reaction, not a vote.
Record the qualitative pass as input to the decision, not as the decision itself.

test.method: Track hit rate of concepts chosen this way against concepts chosen on excitement alone

title: Try a change of presentation before concluding demand is absent
hypothesis: If we try a change of presentation before concluding a product has no demand, then more products with genuine underlying demand survive because low trial can be a packaging or format problem, not a demand problem.
does_not_apply_when: The product already failed the demand or margin checks before any spend, not just a live engagement test

signal.check: A product with demand evidence from its checks is showing low trial or flat engagement in market, and the team is about to conclude no demand exists.

expected_effect.size: unknown, framed by a format change example, not a measured lift

risk.note: Do not over-engineer the fix; try one simple change to presentation or format before further conclusions.

prerequisites: A product that passed demand and margin checks but shows low engagement live
steps: Confirm the product passed the demand and margin checks before live testing.
Identify one simple change to format, packaging or presentation that removes friction.
Test the changed presentation before dropping the product entirely.
If the change still does not move engagement, treat the product as a genuine no-go.

test.method: Compare engagement before and after the presentation change

title: Run market-level questions before product-level questions in the validation pass
hypothesis: If we run market-level questions, demand, competitors, direction, offline availability and target customer, before product-level questions, then wasted product-detail work falls because market-level red flags can kill an idea before unit economics are ever modeled.

signal.check: A validation pass is starting with pricing or sourcing questions before demand, competition and market direction have been checked.

risk.note: None; this only reorders an existing checklist.

prerequisites: A candidate ready for the full validation pass
steps: Answer the market-level questions first: demand size, competitors, market direction, offline availability, target customer.
Stop and drop the candidate if a market-level answer is a clear red flag.
Only proceed to product-level questions, price, margin, SKU count, durability, once market-level questions pass or caution.

test.method: Track time spent on candidates that were later dropped, comparing market-first versus product-first sequencing

title: Score every validation question pass, caution or red flag
hypothesis: If we score every validation question as pass, caution or red flag instead of a strict pass or fail, then more real candidates survive because some flags are fixable through branding or a better formula, not automatic no-gos.

signal.check: A candidate is being judged strictly pass or fail on the validation questions instead of scored pass, caution or red flag with reasons.

expected_effect.size: one example proceeded with 2 red flags judged fixable by branding and formula changes

risk.note: No source gives a weighting or a flag count that automatically kills a product; use the ecomOS hard-stop gate for that instead.

prerequisites: The full set of validation questions answered for the candidate
steps: Score each of the validation questions pass, caution or red flag with the evidence behind it.
Write a highlights and concerns summary at the end.
For each concern, judge it fixable, such as branding or formulation, or market-dependent.
Apply the separate hard-stop gate for margin, regulatory and owned-difference checks regardless of this score.

test.method: Track hit rate of candidates approved with cautions judged fixable versus those dropped outright

title: Run the full validation stack on every candidate regardless of its source
hypothesis: If we run the full validation stack on every candidate regardless of where it came from, a human, another agent, or any scouting method, then no product skips a check because of who or what suggested it.

signal.check: A candidate sourced from a human suggestion or another agent is being fast-tracked past the standard demand, competition, margin and regulatory checks.

risk.note: None; this only removes a fast-track exception.

prerequisites: Any candidate entering the pipeline, from any source
steps: Treat every candidate the same regardless of source: competitors making money, problem or passion, demand proof, sourcing and margin, open angle, then build.
Run the same checklist and scoring for a human-suggested candidate as for one found by an agent or a scouting method.
Log the source method alongside the score for later analysis.

test.method: Track hit rate by candidate source to confirm no source is systematically skipping checks
test.read_point: quarterly review of the research log

title: Log every rule override with the exact signal that justified it
hypothesis: If we log every rule override with the exact number or signal that justified it and cap overrides per memo, then decisions stay consistent because 2 researchers reach the same pick from the same data instead of diverging on unwritten judgment calls.

signal.check: A researcher is breaking a screening rule on conviction without writing down the specific signal that justified the override.

expected_effect.size: 1 override per amber check allowed; no override on margin, regulatory or owned-difference hard stops

risk.note: A memo with more than 2 overrides should be marked a conviction pick and get a human sign-off before proceeding.

prerequisites: A candidate where an amber-level check is being overridden
steps: Allow at most 1 override per amber-level check, with the overriding number or signal written in the log.
Never override a red result on the margin gate, the regulatory check, or the owned-difference requirement.
Flag any memo with more than 2 overrides as a conviction pick needing human sign-off.
Review logged overrides periodically to see if a threshold itself needs recalibrating.

test.method: Track hit rate of overridden candidates against non-overridden ones
test.read_point: after each overridden candidate's first test

title: Diagnose ads and funnel before blaming the product after a failed test
hypothesis: If we diagnose ad metrics and then funnel metrics before concluding a product is wrong after 1 failed test, then fewer good products get killed early because the source's own data shows most failures trace to ads or funnel, not the product.

signal.check: A product's first paid test came back unprofitable and the team is about to call it a no-go without checking link CPC, CTR, CPM, landing-to-cart and cart-to-purchase first.

expected_effect.size: one operator estimated about 90 percent of failures are ads-related, anecdotal

risk.note: After 2 failed tests with ads and funnel already in range, route the product back to the positioning gap audit or to no-go.

prerequisites: Results of the first short paid test, with ad and funnel metrics available
steps: Check link CPC first against the brand's own historical range.
Check CTR next; a low CTR usually points to the creative, not the product.
Check CPM if CTR looks fine but CPC is still high.
Check landing-to-cart and cart-to-purchase rates; only return to the product itself if ads and funnel are both within the brand's normal range.

test.method: Track how many products killed after 1 failed test would have passed on a second test with a fixed ad or funnel issue
test.read_point: after the diagnosis and any resulting retest

title: Require every product claim to be provable before it reaches the shortlist
hypothesis: If we require every benefit, ingredient or outcome claim in a candidate's angle to be provable from the brand's own evidence, then legal and trust risk falls because no shortlist entry can promise an outcome the brand cannot back up.

signal.check: A candidate's proposed angle includes a benefit, ingredient or outcome claim with no evidence behind it from the brand's own testing or sourcing.

risk.note: An unprovable claim risks regulatory action and loss of buyer trust if challenged.

prerequisites: A draft angle or claim for the candidate
steps: List every benefit, ingredient or outcome claim in the draft angle.
For each claim, name the evidence that backs it: a test result, a certificate, a cited study.
Remove or rewrite any claim with no backing evidence before it reaches the shortlist.
Re-check claims against country-specific rules for the category.

test.method: Track how many shortlisted angles needed a claim removed or softened at legal or compliance review

title: Require a named owned difference on every candidate before it can reach go
hypothesis: If we require every candidate to name at least one owned difference, avatar, offer, formulation, spec, packaging or geography, before it can reach a go decision, then the brand never launches a pure copy because a competitor selling item X is a demand signal for the category, not permission to replicate it.

signal.check: A candidate is approaching a go decision with no owned difference named against the competitors it is compared to.

risk.note: This is a hard stop with no override, regardless of business model.

prerequisites: A candidate that has cleared demand and competition checks
steps: List the candidate's avatar, offer structure, formulation, spec, packaging and geography options.
Name at least 1 genuine difference from every identified competitor.
Confirm competitor ads, text, logos, faces or video are never reused as assets.
Block the candidate from a go decision until an owned difference is named.

test.method: Track conversion and hit rate of launches with a clearly named owned difference against ones without

title: Replace every default threshold with the brand's own measured numbers
hypothesis: If we replace every source-given threshold, margin floor, delivery days, refund rate, conversion rate, AOV, with the brand's own measured numbers as soon as they exist, then decisions get more accurate over time because a source's self-reported figures are placeholders, not the brand's reality.
does_not_apply_when: A brand new store with no test history yet to replace the placeholder numbers

signal.check: A go or no-go decision still uses a source's example number, such as a margin floor or CPA target, instead of the brand's own measured figure.

risk.note: None; this only replaces an assumption with real data as it becomes available.

prerequisites: At least 1 completed product test with real CPA, margin or delivery data
steps: List every threshold currently used from this playbook: margin floor, price band, CPA bar, delivery days, refund rate.
After each test, check whether the brand's own measured number differs from the source default.
Update the brand's overlay record with its own number wherever a difference is found.
Mark any memo still using a source's placeholder number as provisional.

test.method: Track how far source-default thresholds drift from the brand's own measured numbers over successive tests

title: Gate on contribution margin after all real costs, not gross margin alone
hypothesis: If we gate a candidate on contribution margin after landed cost, fulfillment, processing and expected refunds instead of gross margin alone, then fewer products that look profitable on paper actually lose money because gross margin ignores real operating costs.

signal.check: A candidate has passed the gross margin and 3x checks but has not had fulfillment, processing and refund costs subtracted to reach a contribution margin figure.

expected_effect.size: must be at or above the brand's own contribution target; mark provisional if no target exists yet

risk.note: Where the brand has no contribution target yet, state the assumption and mark the memo provisional.

prerequisites: Gross margin and 3x multiple already passed
Fulfillment, processing and refund rate figures from the brand's own data
steps: Start from the gross margin figure that already passed the dollar and multiple gates.
Subtract pick, pack and outbound shipping cost per order.
Subtract payment processing rate and expected refund rate from the brand's own history.
Compare the result against the brand's contribution margin target, or mark the memo provisional if none exists yet.

test.method: Track actual contribution margin per order against the pre-launch projection

title: Require positive ad-cost headroom before greenlighting a product
hypothesis: If we require contribution margin minus the brand's historical CPA for similar products to be positive before greenlighting, then a product is not launched with margin that paid acquisition will consume before the brand ever profits.
does_not_apply_when: A brand new store with no CPA history yet for any similar product

signal.check: A candidate has passed the contribution margin gate but its margin has not been checked against the brand's historical CPA for similar products.

expected_effect.size: ad cost headroom must be positive

risk.note: A new store with no CPA history must estimate conservatively and revise once real data exists.

prerequisites: Contribution margin already calculated
The brand's historical CPA for similar products
steps: Pull the brand's average CPA for the closest comparable products already tested.
Subtract that CPA from the candidate's contribution margin.
Require the result to be positive before approving a go decision.
For a brand new store with no CPA history, use a conservative category estimate and mark it provisional.

test.method: Track actual CPA against the assumed CPA used in the headroom calculation

title: Run a quick 10-point screen before spending research tool time
hypothesis: If we run a quick 10-point screen on every candidate before spending paid tool time or deep research on it, then research hours are spent only on candidates likely to survive, because the screen catches obvious drops in minutes.

signal.check: A candidate is going straight into deep demand and competition research without first passing a quick screen on problem, value, business model fit, offline scarcity, weight, content feasibility and regulatory red flags.

risk.note: A quick screen can misjudge a candidate that needs a deeper look; treat a fail here as a strong lean, not an absolute rule.

prerequisites: A candidate just entering the pipeline
steps: Check it solves a felt problem or serves a passionate community, and is not just a novelty.
Check business model fit, offline scarcity, weight and size, and whether content or a demo is feasible.
Check for any fandom, licensing or obvious regulatory red flag.
Log the candidate with its screen result before deciding whether to spend deeper research time.

test.method: Track how many candidates that pass the quick screen also pass the full validation stack

title: Confirm every hard stop is clear before spending on samples or ads
hypothesis: If we explicitly confirm the margin gates, regulatory check and owned-difference requirement are all clear before spending on samples or ads, then no product moves forward on an unnoticed red flag.

signal.check: A candidate is about to receive sample or ad spend without an explicit final check that the margin gates, regulatory clearance and owned-difference requirement are all clear.

risk.note: None; this only adds a final confirmation step before spend.

prerequisites: A candidate that has completed the validation pass
steps: Confirm gross margin, price-to-cost multiple and contribution margin all passed.
Confirm regulatory and IP clearance is documented for every target country.
Confirm an owned difference is named and provable claims are in place.
Only release sample or ad spend once all 3 are confirmed clear.

test.method: Track how many products that failed a hard stop after spend would have been caught by this confirmation step

title: Confirm the full research stack actually ran before greenlighting launch
hypothesis: If we confirm the full research stack, demand, competition, revenue estimate, economics, sourcing, actually ran and is logged before greenlighting a launch, then a rushed or partial validation cannot slip through under time pressure.

signal.check: A launch is about to be approved without an explicit check that every stage of the research stack was completed and logged.

risk.note: None; this only confirms process completion before a launch decision.

prerequisites: A candidate at the final go or no-go stage
steps: Check the research log confirms demand, competition, revenue estimate, economics and sourcing steps are all recorded.
Confirm any overrides used are logged with their justifying signal.
Block the launch decision until every stage shows a recorded result, not a blank.

test.method: Track how many launches later ran into a problem that a missing research stage would have caught

title: Check whether a recommendation source has a financial interest before trusting it
hypothesis: If we check whether a tool, supplier or platform recommendation comes from a source with a financial interest in it before trusting the recommendation, then fewer sourcing or tooling decisions are made on biased advice.

signal.check: A supplier, sourcing platform or research tool is being chosen mainly on a creator or influencer's recommendation with no check on their financial interest.

risk.note: None; this only adds a due-diligence step before acting on a recommendation.

prerequisites: A recommendation for a supplier, platform or tool
steps: Search for whether the recommender has an affiliate link, referral bonus or paid partnership with the recommended platform.
If a financial interest exists, compare at least 1 independent alternative before deciding.
Weight the recommendation as marketing, not neutral advice, when a financial interest is confirmed.

test.method: Track outcomes of decisions made on financially-interested recommendations versus independently verified ones

title: Build a staged offer ladder that lifts AOV without inventing claims
hypothesis: If we build a staged offer ladder, base price, bundle, BOGO or free-gift threshold, tied to provable benefits, then AOV rises in a controlled way because each rung is added only once the base offer and margin are proven.

signal.check: The store has a single base price with no staged bundle, BOGO or free-gift structure planned for test, proven and scaled phases.

expected_effect.size: AOV about 20 to 40 percent above base price, up to about 50 percent for a one-product store

risk.note: Any named ingredient or format claim inside a bundle must be provable before use.

prerequisites: A base price that already passed the margin gate
steps: Define the base single-item price and its margin at that price.
Design the test-stage offer: a simple bundle or multi-buy at a defined discount.
Design the proven-stage offer: a named bundle, BOGO or free-gift threshold once the base sells.
Recalculate margin at each rung's effective price, not the sticker price, before adding it.

test.method: Track AOV at each stage of the offer ladder as it rolls out
test.read_point: 30 days after each new rung launches

title: Set a post-launch review date and metric before starting a test
hypothesis: If we set the post-launch review date and the metric that decides before a test even starts, then the go or continue decision is made on a plan, not on whichever day someone happens to check the numbers.

signal.check: A product test is launching with no review date or decision metric written down in advance.

risk.note: None; this only sets a decision point in advance.

prerequisites: A test about to launch
steps: Write the review date before the test launches, such as 2 to 3 days for a dropshipping-style test, or the brand's own review window.
Name the specific metric that decides continue, pivot or kill at that review point.
Assign who owns reading the result on that date.
Do not let the review slip past the planned date without a decision being made.

test.method: Track how often review dates are actually kept and a decision made on time

title: Assign a named owner for post-test diagnosis before launch
hypothesis: If we assign a named owner for post-test diagnosis before a test launches, then a failed test gets diagnosed promptly because no one is waiting for someone else to pick it up.

signal.check: A test is launching with no named person responsible for running the post-test diagnosis if it underperforms.

risk.note: None; this only assigns clear ownership.

prerequisites: A test about to launch
steps: Name the person responsible for running the post-test diagnosis before the test starts.
Confirm they know the review date and the metric that triggers the diagnosis.
Record the assignment in the launch readiness checklist.

test.method: Track time from a failed test result to a completed diagnosis with an assigned owner versus without one

title: Score every shortlisted candidate on five dimensions and rank before testing
hypothesis: If we score every shortlisted candidate 0 to 3 on demand, competition, angle, economics and logistics and rank by total, then the team tests the strongest candidates first instead of whichever one was researched most recently.

signal.check: Candidates are being picked for testing in the order they were researched rather than ranked by a consistent score across dimensions.

expected_effect.size: 0 to 3 points each on 5 dimensions, 15 points max

risk.note: A red result on the margin gate or regulatory check should set the score to 0 regardless of the rest.

prerequisites: A shortlist of candidates that cleared the initial screens
steps: Score each candidate 0 to 3 on demand, competition, angle, economics and logistics.
Set the score to 0 outright for any red on the margin gate or regulatory check.
Sum the score to a 15-point maximum and rank the shortlist by total.
List any overrides used under the relevant candidate's row.

test.method: Track hit rate of top-ranked candidates tested first against lower-ranked ones tested later
test.read_point: after 5 or more ranked candidates are tested

title: Write a one-page go or no-go memo with evidence before any sourcing spend
hypothesis: If we write a one-page go or no-go memo with the decision, evidence and next owner before any sourcing spend, then everyone acting on the decision works from the same evidence instead of a verbal call.

signal.check: A go decision is being made verbally or informally with no written memo naming the decision, the evidence and the next owner.

risk.note: None; this only formalizes an existing decision into a written, shareable form.

prerequisites: A candidate that has completed the validation stack
steps: Write the decision, go, conditional go or no-go, and the 3 main reasons at the top of the memo.
Attach the demand, competition and economics evidence with numbers and dates.
List any overrides used with their justifying signal.
Name the next owner for each handoff: creative, media, web or operations.

test.method: Track how often a handoff owner has to ask follow-up questions when a written memo exists versus when the decision was only verbal

title: Ask which warehouse produces the better-quality version in an agent sourcing model
hypothesis: If we ask a sourcing agent which of their warehouses produces the better-quality version of the product, then defect and return rates fall because agent models often route the same product through multiple factories of varying quality.
does_not_apply_when: A store sourcing directly from a single named manufacturer, not through a multi-warehouse agent

signal.check: A private sourcing agent is being used and it is unclear which of their warehouses actually produces the better-quality version of the product.

risk.note: None; this only adds a clarifying question to an existing agent relationship.

prerequisites: An active or candidate sourcing agent relationship
steps: Ask the agent directly which warehouse or factory produces the higher-quality version of the product.
Request the sample from that named warehouse specifically.
Confirm future orders route through the same named warehouse before scaling volume.

test.method: Track defect and return rate by warehouse source once orders scale
test.read_point: after the first 100 units from the confirmed warehouse

title: Test random un-niched products only to dodge high CPMs in brand-heavy verticals
hypothesis: If a no-inventory reseller tests random, un-niched products instead of entering brand-heavy verticals such as beauty or dog products, then CPMs stay lower because an unbranded seller cannot compete on ad cost against branded incumbents there.
does_not_apply_when: A brand holding inventory with a fixed category and reputation to build

signal.check: A no-inventory, fast-testing store is picking candidates mainly from high-CPM, brand-heavy verticals with no category focus strategy.

expected_effect.size: unknown, described as by no means a must-do

risk.note: This is an optional beginner path for a no-inventory reseller, not a strategy for a brand building reputation in a fixed category.

prerequisites: A no-inventory, fast-cycle testing model with no fixed category commitment
steps: List verticals known for high CPMs from heavy branded competition, such as women's beauty or dog products.
Deprioritize candidates from those verticals when testing as an unbranded seller.
Favor candidates from lower-competition, less brand-saturated categories instead.
Revisit this rule once the store has its own brand and reputation, since it no longer applies.

test.method: Compare average CPM on candidates from brand-heavy verticals against other categories
test.read_point: after each product's short paid test

title: Require at least one other seller already making money before copying a resale product
hypothesis: If a no-inventory reseller requires at least 1 other seller to already be moving a product profitably before sourcing the same item, then wasted ad spend on unproven items falls because this is the primary viability filter above problem or demand alone.
does_not_apply_when: An owned brand entering a category with no identical competitor yet

signal.check: A no-inventory reseller is sourcing an item with no other seller confirmed to already be selling it profitably.

risk.note: For an owned brand, 0 to 1 identical competitors is the best case instead, per the competitor ladder.

prerequisites: A candidate under consideration for direct resale
steps: Confirm at least 1 other seller is actively running the identical item.
Run the competitor revenue estimate to confirm they are making money, not just testing.
Drop the candidate for resale if no other seller can be confirmed profitable on it.

test.method: Track hit rate of resale candidates with a confirmed profitable seller against ones without

title: Hand the candidate avatar list to creative testing instead of testing avatars here
hypothesis: If product research delivers only the candidate avatar list and gap evidence and hands avatar-versus-avatar creative testing to the creative team, then each team's time is spent on what it does best because testing several avatars in ad creative is a separate skill from finding the gap.

signal.check: The product research process is trying to test several avatars in ad creative itself instead of handing a ranked avatar list to the creative team.

risk.note: None; this only clarifies which team owns avatar creative testing.

prerequisites: A completed positioning gap audit with 3 to 5 candidate avatars
steps: Complete the positioning gap audit and list 3 to 5 candidate avatars with their gap evidence.
Hand the list, with the budget available to test several angles at once, to the creative testing team.
Stop product research involvement at the handoff; do not build or run avatar-versus-avatar ad tests inside this workflow.

test.method: Track time from a completed avatar list to a live creative test with and without this clean handoff

title: Screen a category for jargon it forces buyers to already know
hypothesis: If we screen a candidate category for jargon or forced technical explanation, then a simplified entrant converts better because buyers spend less effort feeling confident about the purchase.
does_not_apply_when: A category with no incumbent using jargon or forced technical explanation

signal.check: Incumbent packaging, PDPs or ads force the buyer to already know a technical term, ingredient name or spec to understand what the product does or why it helps them.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source's own read, not measured

risk.note: A category can be technical for a real reason, such as a regulated claim, that a simplified entrant still cannot skip.

prerequisites: A shortlist of candidate categories to scan
steps: List every incumbent's packaging, PDP or ad copy in the category.
Mark each place a buyer must already know a technical term to understand the benefit.
Score the category high on complexity if buyers need outside knowledge to evaluate the product with confidence.
Treat a high score as an opening to relabel the same benefit by outcome instead of ingredient or spec.

test.method: Compare PDP-to-cart conversion of outcome-led copy against the category's typical spec-led copy
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Build a checkable origin story when the product itself cannot differ
hypothesis: If we build the brand around a real, checkable origin or sourcing story instead of the physical product, then a commodity or white-labeled item converts and repeats better because buyers get a reason to feel good about the purchase the product alone cannot give them.
does_not_apply_when: An origin story that cannot be verified: a fictional or aesthetic-only account is a trust risk if discovered

signal.check: The candidate is a commodity or white-labeled product where competitors sell a near-identical physical item, and no product-level differentiation is available.

risk.note: A fictional or exaggerated origin story is constructed authenticity, a real trust risk if a buyer finds out.

prerequisites: A real, verifiable fact about the product's sourcing, maker or process
steps: Find a real, verifiable fact about where or how the product is made.
Write the origin story only from facts the brand can prove if asked.
Use the story on the PDP and in creative instead of claiming the product itself is different.
Flag internally that this is a trust lever, not a product fix, and never invent a detail.

test.method: A or B a PDP with the origin story against a PDP without it
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Watch real shoppers in the aisle or on live search results
hypothesis: If we watch real shoppers in the physical aisle or scrolling live search results for a candidate category, then category and positioning picks improve because friction and confusion surface that a spy tool's data never shows.
does_not_apply_when: A category with no physical retail presence and no way to observe live shopping behavior

signal.check: The team has only screened a candidate category through ad-spy tools or trend data and has never watched a real buyer shop it.

risk.note: A small number of observed shoppers can be a biased sample.

prerequisites: Access to a physical store or a live search results page for the category
steps: Stand in the aisle, or scroll the live search results, for the candidate category.
Watch for visible hesitation, comparison behavior or questions asked out loud.
Note the concrete friction: hard to shop, confusing labels, uninspiring options.
Translate the friction into a design or positioning question the brand could answer differently.

test.method: Log friction notes from 5 to 10 observed shopping sessions and check whether the resulting positioning change improves conversion after launch

title: Run a time-boxed research-to-concept sprint, not open browsing
hypothesis: If we run a fixed, time-boxed research-to-concept sprint instead of open-ended browsing, then a testable concept ships faster because a deadline forces the team to narrow and commit instead of researching indefinitely.
does_not_apply_when: A team of 1 with no separate design or creative resource to hand a brief to overnight

signal.check: Product research has run past a set window with no candidate concept committed to a decision.

risk.note: A hard deadline can force a weaker pick if the research window was too short for the category.

prerequisites: A separate person or team who can turn a brief into a concept within the same day or overnight
steps: Set a fixed research window, for example one working day.
Assign each researcher a specific scouting task with a deadline.
At the end of the window, pick the strongest 1 to 3 ideas found and write a brief for each.
Hand the brief to design or creative to turn around a testable concept within 24 hours, then decide.

test.method: Compare time from research start to first live test between sprint-run candidates and open-ended ones
test.read_point: after 3 to 5 candidates run each way

title: State the single sharpest reason a candidate differs, not a list
hypothesis: If a go or no-go memo states one concrete, provable reason the candidate differs instead of stacking several reasons, then reviewers and buyers act faster because a single clear reason is easier to repeat and believe than a list.
does_not_apply_when: A candidate with no single strong difference yet, where stacking weaker reasons would only hide that gap

signal.check: The go or no-go memo or pitch lists several different reasons the product is better instead of naming the one difference that matters most.

risk.note: Forcing a single reason too early can hide a real multi-part advantage worth testing.

prerequisites: A completed validation pass with at least one proven point of difference
steps: List every claimed reason the candidate is different or better.
Pick the one reason backed by the strongest evidence.
Rewrite the memo or pitch around that single reason and a concrete before-to-after scenario.
Drop or footnote the other reasons instead of stacking them in the headline.

test.method: Compare reviewer or buyer decision time on memos using 1 stated reason against memos stacking several
test.read_point: next 5 to 10 go or no-go memos

title: Measure and cut the time to a customer's first moment of delight
hypothesis: If we measure and cut the time between a customer's first arrival and their first genuine moment of delight, then early engagement and conversion rise because friction before that moment loses buyers who would have loved the product if they had reached it.
does_not_apply_when: A purchase path with no meaningful onboarding, sampling or demo moment before checkout, such as a single-SKU impulse buy

signal.check: The path from a customer's first arrival, landing page, unboxing or first use, to their first real moment of delight has never been mapped or timed.

expected_effect.size: unknown, borrowed framework, not a tested ecommerce benchmark

risk.note: Over-engineering the delight moment can make it feel gimmicky instead of shortening perceived time.

prerequisites: A mapped customer journey from first arrival to first real product experience
steps: Map every step between first arrival and the first moment the customer feels the product's core benefit.
Time or count the steps in that gap today.
Cut or combine steps that do not lead directly to that moment.
Re-measure the gap and watch early engagement or first-session conversion.

test.method: A or B a shortened first-experience path against the current one
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Give a small immediate payoff during an unavoidable wait
hypothesis: If we give a small immediate sensory or content payoff during an unavoidable wait, such as checkout processing or the ship-to-delivery window, then customers perceive the wait as shorter and drop-off or complaints during that wait fall.
does_not_apply_when: A wait so short it is not noticed, where adding a payoff step would only slow things down

signal.check: A checkout, quiz, order-confirmation or delivery wait has no small payoff, and customers show drop-off, complaints or support tickets during it.

risk.note: The payoff must stay small; over-engineering it can make a good moment feel forced.

prerequisites: An identified unavoidable wait in the customer journey
steps: Find a wait in the journey the customer cannot skip, such as checkout processing or delivery.
Design one small, immediate payoff for that wait, such as a short video, an early tip or a tracking update.
Keep the payoff small and fast, not a distraction from the main path.
Measure drop-off or complaint rate during that wait before and after.

test.method: Compare drop-off or support tickets during the wait before and after adding the payoff
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window

title: Name a brand from one emotional word, tested for instant recall
hypothesis: If we name a brand or product line from one emotional word tied to its outcome and test finalists for instant, no-debate recognition, then brand recall rises because the name is simple to say, remember and repeat.
does_not_apply_when: A market where the category name itself is the strongest signal, such as a generic or technical B2B product

signal.check: A naming decision is being made from category vocabulary or a personal favorite list instead of a single word tied to the product's outcome.

risk.note: Changing a name after launch has real switching cost, so confirm trademark and domain availability before committing.

prerequisites: The product's ultimate emotional outcome or goal stated in one word
steps: Write the single word that captures the product's ultimate emotional outcome, not its category function.
Generate name candidates that start from that word, not from category vocabulary.
Test each finalist for an instant, no-debate reaction from the team.
Confirm trademark and domain availability before committing to the top choice.

test.method: Ask 5 to 10 target buyers to recall the name after a single exposure and compare finalists

title: Confirm a new fulfillment app is a real shipping location pre-launch
hypothesis: If we verify a newly connected fulfillment or 3PL app is registered as an actual shipping location in the store platform before launch, then checkout failures on that product fall because the storefront can otherwise show out of stock or block add to cart even though the app is installed.
does_not_apply_when: A fulfillment method that ships from the store's own existing, already-configured location

signal.check: A new fulfillment or 3PL app was just installed and connected for a product, but no one has confirmed it is added as a shipping location in the platform's settings.

risk.note: This is a launch checklist item, so risk is limited to the time spent checking.

prerequisites: A newly connected fulfillment or 3PL app for at least one product
steps: After installing a fulfillment or 3PL app, open the platform's shipping settings.
Confirm the app is added as an actual shipping location, not just installed.
Add a test product to cart and complete a test checkout before launch.
Fix and re-test immediately if the product shows out of stock or blocks add to cart.

test.method: Run a test checkout on every newly connected fulfillment app before its first live order
test.read_point: before launch and after any new fulfillment app connection

title: Splice the brand's own validated hook into a longer new UGC body
hypothesis: If we cut the opening seconds of the brand's own validated organic video into a longer, newly shot UGC or creator body instead of reusing the full original clip, then paid creative converts better because a proven attention-grabbing open is paired with a more persuasive middle built for the paid platform.
does_not_apply_when: No validated organic hook exists yet that the brand itself owns or can legally reuse

signal.check: The brand has a validated, high-performing organic video, but the plan is either to invent a new hook from scratch or to reuse the full original clip untouched as a paid ad.

risk.note: Only the brand's own validated content or an original creator body qualifies; never splice or reuse a competitor's video, text, logo or face.

prerequisites: A validated organic hook the brand owns or has full rights to reuse
steps: Identify the first few seconds of the brand's own validated, highest-performing organic video.
Brief a creator or editor to build a longer, original body picking up from that same opening idea.
Cut the validated hook into the new longer edit rather than reusing the full original clip.
Test the spliced version against a from-scratch creative on the same offer.

test.method: A or B the spliced creative against a from-scratch creative on the same offer
test.read_point: after the brand's standard test window
